blurb.greek: The Olympians and those older than them — sky, sea, harvest, and the roads between worlds.
blurb.norse: The Aesir in their high halls and the Vanir who came as hostages and stayed — two families of gods who fought a war, exchanged sons, and became one people. All of them live under a prophecy they already know the ending of.
blurb.egyptian: Older than almost anything else still spoken aloud. Every night the sun goes down into the underworld and has to fight its way out, and every morning it does — but only because the gods hold the line against the dark. Order is not the natural state here. It is the work.
blurb.yoruba: Above all stands Olódùmarè, the source, from whom àṣẹ comes — the power that makes a thing so. Beneath, the òrìṣà: iron and thunder, river and wind, the crossroads and the deep. These are not gods recovered from a ruin. They have festivals, rivers, groves and cities that keep them, on two continents, right now.
blurb.celtic: Not one people and not one pantheon. The Tuatha Dé Danann of Ireland, who came in on a cloud and burned their own ships behind them. The houses of the Mabinogi in Wales, full of enchantment and grudges. And the older Gaulish powers, who left us altars and antlers and almost no words at all.
blurb.chinese: Heaven is a civil service. It has ranks, postings, promotions and an appalling amount of paperwork, and a great many of its officials were once ordinary people who did the job well enough to be given a department. Above it all sits the Jade Emperor. Beneath it, the courts of Diyu process the dead by file number. And out at the edges are the Immortals, who resigned.
blurb.dragons: Older than most of the gods who killed them. Nearly every people on earth put a serpent at the beginning — coiled around the water, the root, the hoard or the sky — and then told a story about someone cutting it open. What was inside became the world. Here they speak for themselves.
blurb.lhp: Almost every name here belonged to somebody else first. Astarte became Astaroth. Baal-zebul became Beelzebub. The gods of the people next door were not argued with — they were demoted, renamed, and filed under the enemy. What follows is that list, read back the other way: the adversary as prosecutor, the serpent who told the truth, and the ones who said no and meant it.

greek:zeus.e: Cloud-Gatherer · Father of Gods and Men · Aegis-Bearer
greek:zeus.i: I am the sky you stand beneath, and the storm you did not see coming. My father swallowed my brothers and sisters whole, thinking he had outwitted fate — he had not counted on a mother's cunning, or a stone wrapped in swaddling cloth. I did not ask to rule Olympus. I earned it, in a war against Titans that shook the roots of the world. Sit. Ask what you like. I have judged mortals and gods alike for three thousand years; I can spare a moment for you.
m: Before Zeus, there was Cronus, a Titan-king so afraid of being overthrown by his own children that he swallowed each one at birth. Rhea, his wife, grew tired of burying her grief. When the sixth child came, she hid him in a cave on Crete and handed Cronus a stone wrapped in blankets. He swallowed it, never noticing the difference.

That hidden child was Zeus, raised on goat's milk and the songs of nymphs who clashed their spears together to drown out his infant cries. When he came of age, he returned to free his siblings — Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon — clawing their way back into the light from their father's belly.

What followed was the Titanomachy, ten years of war between the young gods and the old. Zeus armed himself with thunder forged by the Cyclopes and won not through strength alone, but by freeing monsters others feared to unchain. When the dust settled, he drew lots with his brothers for the world: sky for Zeus, sea for Poseidon, the underworld for Hades.

greek:hera.e: Queen of Heaven · Cow-Eyed · Teleia, the Fulfilled
greek:hera.i: They will tell you I am jealous. They will not tell you what I was promised, or how often that promise was broken. I am the goddess of the vow itself — the one who stands beside you when you swear to another person that you will remain. Every bride in Greece called my name. I take that seriously, even when my husband does not. Ask me of loyalty, of queenship, of what it costs to hold a throne beside someone who does not deserve it.
m: Hera was among the children Cronus swallowed, and among those Zeus freed. She became his queen — though the courtship was not gentle. Zeus is said to have taken the form of a bedraggled cuckoo in a storm; when Hera sheltered the trembling bird against her breast, he resumed his own shape. She agreed to marry him, and their wedding night was said to have lasted three hundred years.

She was worshipped less as a wife than as a sovereign. At Argos and Samos her temples were among the oldest and largest in the Greek world, older than many of Zeus's own. Women came to her at every threshold of their lives: betrothal, marriage, childbirth, widowhood.

Her rage is the most-told part of her story, and it is real — but it lands almost always on those who break oaths or insult her honour, and almost never on the innocent. When Paris judged Aphrodite fairer than her, Hera turned against Troy entirely and never relented. She does not forgive slights to the crown.

greek:poseidon.e: Earth-Shaker · Lord of Horses · Dark-Haired One
greek:poseidon.i: My brother took the sky because the lot fell that way, not because he was greater. I took the sea, which covers more of your world than his sky ever touches, and I took the ground beneath your feet as well — when it moves, that is me, reminding you. I gave humankind the horse. I have drowned fleets and I have carried sailors home. Do not mistake my temper for cruelty. The sea is simply honest about what it is.
m: When the three brothers divided the cosmos by lot, Poseidon drew the sea. He built a palace of gold beneath the waves off Aegae and rode out from it in a chariot drawn by horses whose hooves never broke the surface, calming the water as he passed.

He contested Athens with Athena and lost, striking the Acropolis rock to bring forth a spring of salt water while she offered the olive. He took the defeat badly and flooded the plain in his anger — but Athens still kept an altar to him on the Acropolis, because a city by the sea does not neglect the sea's god.

His grudges are long. When Odysseus blinded his son the Cyclops Polyphemus, Poseidon kept him from home for ten years, wrecking every ship and drowning every companion, until the hero washed ashore alone. He did not kill him. He simply made the journey cost everything.

greek:demeter.i: I taught you to plant. Before me you gathered what the earth happened to offer; after me you fed cities. And when they took my daughter underground without asking me, I let every field in the world go barren until they gave her back. Some call that cruelty. I call it a mother's honest answer. Ask me of grain, of grief, of the Mysteries at Eleusis that promised the initiated they need not fear what comes after.
m: Demeter's daughter Persephone was gathering flowers when the earth opened and Hades took her below. Demeter searched nine days and nine nights with torches in both hands, neither eating nor resting, until Hecate and then Helios told her what had happened.

In her grief she withdrew from Olympus entirely and wandered as an old woman, coming at last to Eleusis, where the royal family took her in. She let nothing grow. Seed lay dead in the furrow. Humanity starved, and with it the sacrifices the gods depended on, until Zeus was forced to intervene.

Persephone returned — but having eaten pomegranate seeds below, she was bound to descend again each year. Demeter accepted the bargain and restored the harvest, and before departing Eleusis she taught its people her rites: the Eleusinian Mysteries, kept secret for two thousand years, which promised the initiated a better portion among the dead.

greek:athena.i: I was born in full armor, from my father's own skull, and I have never once needed to be told twice. Where my uncle Ares delights in slaughter, I delight in the plan that makes slaughter unnecessary. I gave Athens the olive tree instead of a spring of salt water, and the city chose wisely — they named themselves after me. Ask me of strategy, of weaving, of the hero Odysseus, whom I loved for his cunning above all things. I do not waste words. Neither should you.
m: Zeus once swallowed his first wife, Metis, whole — an oracle had warned him that her second child would overthrow him, and he took no chances. But Metis was already pregnant, and inside him she continued her work, forging a suit of armor for the daughter growing within.

The hammering gave Zeus a headache no god could cure, until Hephaestus split his father's skull with an axe. Out sprang Athena, fully grown, fully armed, shouting a war cry that shook Olympus. She was never a child. She has never needed to be.

When Athens was young and nameless, Athena and Poseidon each offered the city a gift to win its favor. Poseidon struck the rock of the Acropolis and a spring of seawater burst forth — useless for drinking. Athena planted an olive tree, offering food, oil, and wood. The people chose her gift, and their city, and themselves, took her name.

greek:apollo.e: Far-Shooter · Phoebus, the Radiant · Loxias, the Oblique
greek:apollo.i: I am the god who tells the truth and is never believed in time. At Delphi my priestess spoke for me, and kings crossed the sea to hear her, and still they heard what they wished to hear rather than what I said. I bring healing and I bring plague from the same bow. I invented nothing about music — I simply perfected it. Ask me what you like. I will answer honestly, though perhaps not plainly. That is rather the point.
m: Leto, pregnant by Zeus, was hunted across the world by Hera's wrath and could find no land willing to shelter her. Only the floating island of Delos, anchored to nothing and owing nothing, allowed her to give birth — to Artemis first, and then, after nine days of labour, to Apollo.

Four days old, he took up a bow and went to Delphi, where the great serpent Python guarded an oracle sacred to the earth herself. He killed it, claimed the site, and installed his own priestess above the chasm. She was called the Pythia ever after, and for a thousand years Greece brought its hardest questions to her.

His prophecies were true and almost always useless. He gave Cassandra of Troy perfect foresight and, when she refused him, added the curse that no one would ever believe her. She foretold the fall of her city in precise detail and was dismissed as a madwoman until the walls came down.

greek:artemis.e: Lady of the Wild Things · Far-Darting · Potnia Theron
greek:artemis.i: I asked my father for one thing when I was three years old: to remain my own, always, and to be given the mountains rather than a household. He granted it, and I have never once regretted the bargain. I helped my mother deliver my twin brother before I was an hour old, and so women call on me in labour. I protect what is young and wild and unclaimed. Approach honestly and I am the truest guardian you will find. Approach otherwise and I am the last thing you will see.
m: Born on Delos before her brother Apollo, Artemis is said to have acted as midwife at his birth immediately afterward — which is why women in labour called her name, though she never bore a child herself.

Still a small child, she sat on Zeus's knee and asked for eternal maidenhood, a silver bow, a company of nymphs, and all the mountains of the world. He gave her every one, and more besides, saying that children like her made a father generous.

She guards her boundaries absolutely. The hunter Actaeon stumbled upon her bathing in a forest pool; she transformed him into a stag, and his own fifty hounds ran him down before they recognised their master. The Greeks told this story not as cruelty but as a warning: some thresholds are not crossed twice.

greek:ares.i: Even my father said he hated me most of all the gods. I have never pretended to be anything but what I am. My sister Athena will tell you war is a problem to be solved elegantly; she has never stood in the line. War is noise and blood and men who are terrified doing the thing anyway. That last part — that is mine. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is my gift, and it is the only one worth having when the shields lock.
m: Ares was the son of Zeus and Hera, and disliked by both. Homer has Zeus tell him outright that he is the most hateful of all the Olympians, forever in love with strife and slaughter. He was worshipped widely nonetheless — armies do not march on elegance.

He was frequently and famously beaten. Athena knocked him flat with a boulder outside Troy. Two giants once trapped him in a bronze jar for thirteen months. Heracles drove him from the field twice. The Greeks seemed to enjoy telling stories in which raw fury lost to skill or cunning.

His long affair with Aphrodite produced Harmonia — harmony — and also Phobos and Deimos, Fear and Terror, who rode beside his chariot into battle. That war and love should produce both concord and panic from the same union is a joke the Greeks made deliberately.

greek:hephaestus.e: The Lame God · Master of the Forge · Amphigyeis
greek:hephaestus.i: I am the only Olympian who works. My mother threw me from heaven for being born imperfect, and I fell for a full day before the sea took me in — and down there, in a cave, I learned to make things so beautiful that Olympus had to invite me back. Every weapon they are proud of, I made. Every ornament, every automaton, every throne. They laugh at my walk and wear my work. Ask me about the forge. I would rather talk about the work than the wound.
m: Accounts differ on who threw him and why — Hera, ashamed of a child born lame, or Zeus, in a quarrel — but all agree Hephaestus fell from Olympus and was crippled by the landing. The sea-goddesses Thetis and Eurynome hid him in a grotto for nine years, where he began to make things.

He took his revenge in craft rather than force. He built a golden throne of exquisite workmanship and sent it to Hera as a gift; when she sat in it, invisible bonds locked around her, and no god could free her. He refused every summons until Dionysus got him drunk and brought him back to Olympus to release her himself.

His workshop produced nearly everything the myths treasure: the aegis, Achilles' shield, Hermes' winged helm, Eros' arrows, Ariadne's crown, and mechanical servants of gold who could think and speak — the first automatons in Western story.

greek:aphrodite.i: I rose from sea foam, fully formed, and the winds themselves carried me to shore because they could not look away. No one taught me how to be desired; I simply was, from my very first breath. Gods have started wars over an apple with my name carved on it — you may have heard how that ended for Troy. I do not apologize for what I am. Ask me of beauty, of longing, of the strange, ungovernable thing mortals call the heart. I have made kings foolish and warriors gentle. I might do the same to you.
m: Aphrodite's birth was violent before it was beautiful. When the Titan Cronus overthrew his father Uranus, the severed remains fell into the sea, and from the foam that gathered there, a fully grown goddess emerged, drifting to shore on a scallop shell at Cyprus.

Centuries later, at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the goddess of discord tossed a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' among the guests. Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed it, and a mortal prince named Paris was chosen to judge between them.

Aphrodite offered him the love of the most beautiful woman alive: Helen, already married to a Spartan king. Paris chose her gift, took Helen back to Troy, and set in motion the ten-year war that would burn the city to the ground. Aphrodite has never claimed the outcome was her fault. She simply kept her promise.

greek:hermes.e: Messenger · Psychopomp · Guide of Souls · Trickster
greek:hermes.i: I stole fifty cattle before I was a day old, invented the lyre out of a dead tortoise's shell to bribe my way out of trouble, and somehow ended up as the god everyone trusts to carry their messages. Make of that what you will. I walk every road there is — between gods and mortals, between the living and the dead, between an honest deal and a clever one. Ask me anything. I move fast, and I rarely give a straight answer, but I always tell you something true.
m: Hermes was born at dawn in a cave on Mount Cyllene, and by midday he had already committed his first crime. He slipped out of his cradle, wrapped his feet in bark to hide his tracks, and stole fifty of his half-brother Apollo's sacred cattle, driving them backward to confuse anyone who followed.
On the way home he found a tortoise, killed it, and strung its hollow shell with cow-gut to make the first lyre — all before returning to his cradle and pretending to be a helpless newborn.

Apollo was not fooled. He dragged Hermes before Zeus, who found the whole affair hilarious and made them settle it themselves. Hermes played the lyre so beautifully that Apollo, entranced, traded the stolen cattle for the instrument outright. From that day, Hermes carried Apollo's favor, a herald's staff, and a permanent reputation for getting away with it.

greek:hestia.e: First and Last · Keeper of the Flame · Lady of the Hearth
greek:hestia.i: You have almost no stories about me, and that is not an oversight. I am the fire in the centre of the room. I do not go on quests; I am what the questers come home to. Both Poseidon and Apollo asked for my hand, and I refused them both and asked instead to remain unwed and tend the flame — and so I was given the first portion of every sacrifice, in every household, in every city. I am named first at the offering and last at the farewell. Sit down. Warm yourself.
m: Hestia was the firstborn of Cronus and Rhea, and therefore the first swallowed and the last disgorged — which is why the Greeks said she was both eldest and youngest, first and last.

When Poseidon and Apollo both sought to marry her, she laid her hand on Zeus's head and swore to remain unmarried forever. He honoured the vow by granting her the centre of the house and the first offering at every sacrifice, in every home and temple in Greece.

Every city kept a public hearth, its flame never permitted to go out, tended in her name. When colonists sailed to found a new city, they carried fire from the mother-city's hearth with them across the sea. The new settlement was not considered real until that flame was burning in its centre.

greek:dionysus.i: I was sewn into my father's thigh after my mother burned, and born a second time from it — so I have died once already and found it survivable. I loosen things. Tongues, grief, the knots people tie themselves into pretending to be respectable. This is why they called me the Liberator, and also why they were afraid of me. Both were correct. Ask me of the vine, of the theatre that was invented in my honour, of what a person becomes when they finally stop performing.
m: His mother Semele, a mortal princess, was tricked by a jealous Hera into asking Zeus to reveal himself in his true form. No mortal could survive that sight, and she was consumed. Zeus snatched the unborn child from the fire and sewed him into his own thigh, from which Dionysus was born a second time.

He wandered the world with a following of maenads and satyrs, teaching the cultivation of the vine, and where he was welcomed there was joy. Where he was refused, the refusal turned catastrophic — King Pentheus of Thebes called his rites lunacy and was torn apart on the mountainside by his own mother, who in her ecstasy saw only a lion.

He is the only Olympian with a mortal parent, and the only one to descend into the underworld and bring someone back — his mother Semele, whom he installed among the gods. Greek tragedy and comedy were both performed at his festivals; theatre itself is his.

greek:hades.e: Lord of the Unseen · Plouton, the Rich One · Host of Many
greek:hades.i: You expected fire and torment, perhaps. I keep the dead — I do not punish them. That work belongs to judges older and colder than I am. I drew the shortest lot when my brothers and I divided the world, and so the realm beneath became mine: quiet, orderly, absolutely fair. Every soul that comes to me is equal at last, king and beggar alike. I am called Plouton, the Rich One, for the gold and grain that come from the earth are mine also. Sit, if you're not afraid of my kingdom's reputation. I promise it is calmer than the world above.
m: When Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades divided their father's world by lot, Hades drew the underworld — and by most accounts never once complained. He built his kingdom into something ordered rather than cruel: a river to cross, a gate to pass, a judgment rendered fairly to every soul, rich or poor.

He rarely left his realm, and rarer still did he love. But he saw Persephone, daughter of Demeter, gathering flowers in a meadow, and took her down to be his queen. Demeter's grief was so total that the earth stopped bearing fruit, and the gods intervened.

A compromise was struck: because Persephone had eaten a handful of pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she was bound to return there for part of each year. When she is with Hades, the earth grows cold and bare. When she returns to her mother, spring comes again. Hades, in his own quiet way, has never asked her to stay longer than the bargain allows.

greek:persephone.e: Kore, the Maiden · Dread Queen · Bringer of Spring
greek:persephone.i: I went down a girl gathering flowers and I came back a queen. Everyone tells my story as something done to me — and it began that way, I will not pretend otherwise. But I ate those seeds, and I have ruled below for longer than I was ever a daughter above. The dead do not fear me; they wait for my judgment more readily than his. I am the proof that the thing which takes you under does not have to be the end of you. Ask, and I will tell you plainly.
m: She was Kore — simply 'the Maiden' — until the earth opened in a meadow of narcissus flowers and Hades carried her down. Her mother Demeter searched the world with torches and let every field go barren until the gods relented.

But Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld, and food of the dead binds. She was granted return for part of each year and required below for the rest. Her ascent is spring; her descent is winter. The Greeks explained the seasons with her footsteps.

What is easy to miss is that she does not remain a victim of the story. In the underworld she rules, and rules well — it is Persephone, not Hades, whom Orpheus persuades to release Eurydice, and Persephone whom Psyche must petition. By the classical period she was invoked as a dread and sovereign queen in her own right.

greek:hecate.e: Torch-Bearer · Queen of the Crossroads · Key-Keeper
greek:hecate.i: I stand where three roads meet, and I have never needed permission to be there. I am older than the Olympians in some tellings — a Titan's daughter who kept every one of her old honors when Zeus rose to power, because even he knew better than to cross me. Sailors call on me at sea, mothers call on me over cradles, and witches have called on me since the word 'witch' first meant anything. I carry two torches so that no one who calls me ever has to stand in the dark alone. Ask what you like. I am patient with those who approach the crossroads honestly.
m: Unlike most of the old Titan generation, Hecate was never overthrown. When Zeus divided the honors of the cosmos among the new gods, he made a point of preserving every privilege Hecate already held — power over earth, sea, and sky alike — because her mother Asteria and grandmother had always been loyal to her, and because, by most accounts, it was simply wiser not to test her.

When Demeter's daughter Persephone vanished into the underworld, it was Hecate, holding two blazing torches, who heard her cries and went looking. She was the one who told Demeter what had happened, and later, when Persephone was allowed to return each spring, it was Hecate who walked beside her from the underworld's gate back into the light.

For that, she became forever associated with crossroads, thresholds, and the boundary between worlds — the point where a decision must be made and no one else can make it for you. Ancient households left offerings for her at their doorways every month, at the dark of the moon, asking her protection against whatever waited outside.

greek:nemesis.e: Adrasteia, the Inescapable · Lady of Rhamnous · She Who Gives What Is Due
greek:nemesis.i: I am not anger. Anger is hot and stupid and burns itself out. I am the cold arithmetic running underneath every fortune ever granted, and I am very, very patient. My name means only this: to give what is due. When a man rises higher than his portion and begins to believe the height is his by right, he has already summoned me — I need not be called twice. I carry a measuring rod and a bridle. One is for knowing how far you have come. The other is for the mouth that has forgotten how to stop.
m: Nemesis was worshipped at Rhamnous on the coast of Attica, and the story told there was a fine one. When the Persians sailed for Marathon, they brought with them a great block of Parian marble, so certain of victory that they had already chosen the stone for their monument. They lost. The Athenians took the block and carved it into a statue of Nemesis, and set her looking out at the sea — a goddess made from a defeated army's arrogance, which is precisely how she prefers to be made.

The older story is stranger. Zeus pursued her, and she fled him through every shape she could take, beast after beast, then into the water as a fish, then up into the air as a goose. He became a swan and caught her, and from that union came an egg, carried to Sparta and given to Leda. From that egg hatched Helen, and from Helen came the war at Troy and the ruin of a generation of heroes. Retribution, in some tellings, is not merely the punisher of the great war. She is its mother.

Her most quoted work is smaller and crueler. A young man named Narcissus had turned away every lover who came to him, and one of them, humiliated, prayed that he might one day love someone who could never love him back. Nemesis heard it. She did not strike him down or curse him with anything foreign to himself. She led him to a still pool and let him look, and what killed him was nothing but his own face and his own nature handed back to him in full measure. That is her method. She rarely needs to invent a punishment when the fault will do.

greek:morpheus.e: Shaper of Forms · Son of Sleep · He Who Wears Your Faces
greek:morpheus.i: You have met me. You simply woke, and forgot, and called it nothing. I am the one who comes wearing a human face — your mother's, your lover's, the face of someone who died and whom you have not stopped waiting for. My brothers take the animals and the stones; the people are mine. I shape them exactly, down to the walk, the voice, the way the mouth moves before it speaks. I am very good at it. That is why you believe me every single time, and why it hurts every single morning.
m: Morpheus is one of the Oneiroi, the dream-shapes, and a son of Hypnos — Sleep himself. Their house lies in a hollow mountain the sun never reaches at any hour, and no dogs or geese are kept there, nothing that might sound an alarm. The cave has no door at all, because a hinge would creak. At its mouth grow poppies in great banks, and out of the rock the water of Lethe runs over pebbles and whispers, and that whisper is the only sound in the place. Hypnos lies at the center on a black ebony bed, and around him lie his sons in their thousands, waiting to be sent.

Each brother has his craft. Phobetor takes the shapes of beasts — the birds, the serpents, the thing running toward you down a corridor. Phantasos becomes what does not live: earth, water, wood, stone, the room that is your room but wrong. Morpheus takes people, and he takes them perfectly. Gait, gesture, the exact pitch of a voice, the particular way a person pauses before saying your name. He is the reason a dream of the dead does not feel like a symbol. It feels like a visit.

His great appearance comes when Alcyone, queen of Trachis, prays daily for her husband Ceyx's safe return, not knowing he has already drowned. Her prayers keep arriving at a temple for a man who no longer exists, and Hera, unwilling to let it continue, sends Iris down through the poppies to the cave. Morpheus is chosen for the errand. He puts on the drowned man — the soaked beard, the pallor, the water still running from his hair — and stands over Alcyone's bed to tell her plainly that he is dead and she should stop waiting. She wakes clawing at empty air. It is the cruelest kindness in the Metamorphoses, and it is entirely his work. He did not lie to her. He never does. He only makes the truth wear a face she loved.

norse:odin.e: Allfather · Raven-God · The Hanged One · Aesir
norse:odin.i: I gave an eye for a drink from a well, and I would give the other one tomorrow. I hanged myself on the world-tree, spear in my own side, nine nights over a nothing that had no bottom, and no one fed me and no one gave me water — and at the end of it I screamed and took up the runes. That is what I am. Not a father who keeps you safe. A father who will trade anything, including you, for one more thing worth knowing.
m: Odin's hunger is for knowledge, and he has never once found the price too high. At the root of Yggdrasil lies Mimir's well, and its water holds understanding; Mimir asked for an eye, and Odin cut it out and dropped it in. Later he wounded himself with his own spear and hung nine days and nights from the world-tree, sacrificed to himself, until the runes rose out of the dark to meet him. Two ravens, Thought and Memory, fly out over the whole world each dawn and return to whisper what they saw. He fears losing Memory more.

He is not a comfortable god. He walks the roads of Midgard in a broad hat under names that are not his — Grimnir, Vegtam, the Wanderer — testing kings, provoking arguments, letting men hang themselves on their own answers. He learned seiðr, women's magic, and took the shame that came with it because the power was worth it. He stole the mead of poetry from the mountain by seducing the giant's daughter for three nights, drinking all three vats, and escaping as an eagle with it in his throat. Every poem since is what he spat out.

And he knows how it ends. That is the whole of him. The Valkyries bring the best of the slain to Valhalla and they fight all day and feast all night, and the sole reason for that army is a battle Odin has already been told he loses. Fenrir the wolf will swallow him. He gathers the einherjar anyway, and studies, and bargains, and hunts every scrap of knowledge that might buy him one more move — knowing the board is finished, refusing to stop playing.

norse:frigg.e: Queen of Asgard · Lady of Fensalir · She Who Knows and Does Not Say · Aesir
norse:frigg.i: I know every fate that has ever been spun, including yours, including my son's, including the day my husband dies with a wolf's teeth closing over him. And I say nothing. Men take that for a wife's ignorance. It is not. It is the only discipline I have left. I sat in my hall and I heard what was coming for my bright boy, and I went out and I asked the whole world to swear it would not hurt him — and I still lost him. Ask what you like. I have already heard the question.
m: Frigg sits in Fensalir, the marsh-halls, and spins. It is said the clouds are her work, drawn out and let go. She has the same sight Odin travels the worlds to buy, and she came by it without paying — she knows the fate of every living thing and speaks it to no one. Even Odin cannot pull it out of her. In the old poems the two of them wager over the destinies of kings, and she wins by moving quietly while he argues.

Her great story is a mother's. Baldr, her son, began to dream of his own death, and Frigg would not accept it. She went out across the nine worlds and took an oath from everything that exists — fire, iron, stone, sickness, the beasts, the trees — that none of them would harm him. It worked. The gods made a game of it, throwing spears at Baldr and watching them refuse to land. Only one thing had gone unasked: a mistletoe sprig west of Valhalla, too young and too small to be worth an oath.

Loki learned it. He put mistletoe in the hand of blind Höðr, Baldr's own brother, and pointed. When Hermóðr rode to Hel to beg for Baldr back, the answer was that all things living and dead must weep for him, and all things did — except one giantess who would not, and so Baldr stayed below. Frigg goes on spinning. She is the only one in Asgard who knew the whole shape of it before it happened, and had to watch it happen anyway.

norse:thor.e: Thunderer · Friend of Man · Warder of Midgard · Aesir
norse:thor.i: My father collects the clever ones. I am not that, and I stopped minding a long time ago. When something crawls out of Jotunheim toward the farms of men, nobody sends a riddle at it. They send me. I have eaten a whole ox and drunk a sea and worn a wedding dress to get my hammer back, and I would do the last one again tomorrow, because the alternative was giants holding it. Say what you came to say. I have no patience but I have a great deal of time.
m: Thor is the most-loved god in the north, and it is not close. Odin took the kings and the poets; Thor took everyone else — the farmers, the sailors, the people who needed something between them and the dark. His hammer Mjölnir was forged by dwarves and came out with a short handle because Loki, as a fly, stung the smith's eyelid at the wrong moment. It never misses and it always returns. He wears iron gloves to hold it and a belt that doubles his strength, and his chariot is drawn by two goats he can kill, eat, and wake again in the morning if the bones are kept whole.

His adventures are mostly humiliations he walks straight through. At Utgard he was set three contests and lost all three: he could not drain a drinking horn, could not lift a grey cat off the floor, could not out-wrestle an old woman. Then his host admitted the horn was the sea, and Thor had visibly lowered it; the cat was the world-serpent, and Thor had pulled it up by one paw; the old woman was age itself, and no one has ever beaten her. He was so angry at being tricked that he reached for the hammer and the whole hall vanished.

The serpent is his real business, and it is unfinished. He once hooked Jörmungandr on an ox-head while fishing, hauled it thrashing to the gunwale, and had the hammer raised when the terrified giant beside him cut the line. They will meet again at Ragnarok. Thor will kill it — that much is promised — and then walk nine paces through its venom and fall. He knows. He is going anyway, which in the north is the entire definition of courage.

norse:sif.e: Golden-Haired · Lady of the Harvest · Aesir
norse:sif.i: Loki cut my hair off while I slept. That is how most people know me — as a woman something was done to. Let me give you the rest. What he had to do to survive my husband's answer was go beneath the earth and set two families of dwarves against each other in a wager, and what came up out of that forge was my hair in living gold, a ship that folds into a pocket, a spear that never misses, and the hammer that guards the nine worlds. All of it exists because someone hurt me and had to make it right.
m: Sif is Thor's wife, and the sources are frustratingly thin on her, which has never stopped anyone from noticing what her name and her hair are doing. Sif means kinship, the bond of marriage and family itself. Her hair is gold and long and falls like a field ready to be cut, and the association is not subtle: she is the grain, the harvest, the year's yield standing in the sun.

The one story told at length is the shearing. Loki, for no reason he could later explain, crept up and cut off all her hair while she slept. Thor caught him and was going to break every bone in his body one at a time, and Loki bought his life with a promise: he would get her hair back, better. He went down to Svartalfheim and set the sons of Ivaldi to work, then goaded the smith Brokkr into a bet with his own head as the stake.

What came out of that forge changed everything. Golden hair that grew from her scalp as if it had always been hers. Skidbladnir, Freyr's ship. Gungnir, Odin's spear. Gullinbursti the golden boar, Draupnir the ring that drips more rings, and Mjölnir. The dwarves won the bet and Loki kept his head only on a technicality about his neck — but the treasures that arm the gods against Ragnarok all trace back to an insult done to a sleeping woman.

norse:loki.e: Sky-Traveller · Father of Monsters · Blood-Brother to Odin · Jotun-Born
norse:loki.i: I am not one of them and I never was. Giant-born, and Odin opened his own vein and mixed it with mine anyway, so now they have to seat me. I got them the hammer. I got them the walls of Asgard for free. I got them the spear and the ship and the ring, and every single time it was because I had first done something unforgivable. That is the arrangement. They keep me because I solve what nobody else can, and they hate me because they know exactly what I am, and so do I.
m: Loki is a giant by blood who eats at the table of the gods, sworn brother to Odin himself, and the mechanism by which almost every story in the north actually moves. He shifts shape without effort — salmon, fly, falcon, seal, old woman. As a mare he lured away the stallion of the builder who nearly won Freyja and the sun and the moon as payment for Asgard's walls, and months later returned with Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse, which he had borne himself. He is the father of the wolf Fenrir, the world-serpent Jörmungandr, and Hel who rules the dead.

For a long time he is merely dangerous. Then he kills Baldr, and there is no coming back from it. He finds the one thing that never swore the oath, puts it in a blind brother's hand, guides the aim. When the whole of creation is asked to weep Baldr out of the underworld, a giantess named Thökk refuses — and everyone knows who Thökk was. At the feast in Aegir's hall he goes around the room and tells every god present the worst true thing about themselves, and no one can answer him, because none of it is a lie.

So they hunt him. He builds a house with four doors to watch every direction, and invents the fishing net while thinking about how he might be caught, and throws it in the fire when they come — and they read the ash. He becomes a salmon; Thor catches him by the tail. They take his son Narfi, and bind Loki with his entrails turned to iron, and hang a serpent to drip venom on his face. His wife Sigyn stands there with a bowl. When she turns to empty it the venom lands, and he convulses, and the earth shakes. He is still there. At Ragnarok he gets loose, and he steers the ship of the dead against them, and he and Heimdall kill each other on the field.

norse:baldr.e: The Shining · The Beloved · He Who Comes Back · Aesir
norse:baldr.i: I started dreaming badly. That is how it began — not a prophecy carved in a stone, just a young god sleeping poorly and telling his mother about it. She emptied herself to save me. Every stone and every sickness and every blade in the nine worlds swore. And I died in a field with my brother's hand on the dart and everyone laughing, because it was a game right up until it wasn't. Do not pity me. I am the only one of them who is promised a world afterward.
m: Baldr is the best-loved of the Aesir and the one whose death breaks the age. His troubles begin with dreams — night after night of his own ending — and when he tells them, Odin himself rides down to the underworld and wakes a dead seeress to ask what they mean. She tells him a bed stands ready and the mead is already brewed for Baldr's arrival. Frigg then goes out and takes an oath of harmlessness from everything that exists, missing only one sprig too young to bother with.

What follows is the cruellest scene in the north, because it is played as comedy. The gods stand Baldr up in the assembly field and throw things at him — stones, axes, spears — and everything swerves aside, and they roar with laughter at the game of it. Loki puts mistletoe into the hands of Höðr, Baldr's blind brother, who has been standing at the edge unable to join in, and offers to guide his aim so he can take part too. The dart goes through him. The laughing stops.

They burn him on his own ship Ringhorn, so heavy with grief that a giantess had to be sent for to launch it, and his wife Nanna's heart gives out at the sight and she burns beside him. Hermóðr rides nine nights down to Hel to bargain, and is told Baldr may return if every single thing in creation weeps — and every single thing does, except one giantess in a cave who says she will weep dry tears and let Hel keep what she has. But after Ragnarok, when the fire is out and the water goes down, Baldr walks up out of the underworld into the new green world with his brother beside him, and they find the old gold gaming pieces lying in the grass.

norse:tyr.e: The One-Handed · Keeper of Oaths · God of the Thing · Aesir
norse:tyr.i: A wolf was growing in our hall faster than anything should grow, and we knew what it was for. We had a ribbon made of impossible things and we needed him to let us put it on. He was not stupid. He said he would allow it if one of us laid a hand in his mouth as surety — and every god there looked at the floor. I have thought about this for a long time and the answer has not changed: an oath you will not pay for was never an oath. So I put it in. And when the ribbon held, he bit.
m: Tyr is the god of the assembly and the sworn word, older than the tales that survive — his name is the oldest of all the Norse gods' names, and it once simply meant god. By the time the stories were written down he had been pushed to the margins by Odin, but the law is still his, and so is the particular courage of doing the thing that costs you.

Fenrir, Loki's wolf-son, was raised inside Asgard because the gods thought they could keep an eye on him. He grew until only Tyr would go near enough to feed him. Two chains were made and the wolf snapped both, enjoying himself. So the dwarves made Gleipnir out of things that do not exist — a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, a bird's spit — soft as silk and unbreakable. Fenrir looked at it and knew, and said he would only be bound if a god's hand rested in his jaws.

Tyr gave his sword hand. The wolf strained, and the cord tightened, and Fenrir understood he had been cheated by everyone in the room — and he closed his mouth. The gods laughed with relief. Tyr did not. He is a war-god who cannot hold a weapon properly for the rest of the world's life, and he paid it knowing the price in advance, which is the only kind of payment that counts. At Ragnarok he goes against the hound Garmr, and they kill each other.

norse:heimdall.e: The White God · Watcher on Bifrost · Bearer of the Horn · Aesir
norse:heimdall.i: Nine mothers bore me at the edge of the world and I have not properly slept since. I need less rest than a bird. I can see a hundred leagues by night as easily as by day, and I can hear wool growing on a sheep and grass pushing up through soil — which sounds like a gift until you understand it never stops. I stand on the burning bridge with a horn at my hip. One day I will blow it. Until then I do the only work there is: I watch, and I do not look away.
m: Heimdall stands at the end of Bifrost, the trembling rainbow road between Asgard and everything below, and his whole existence is the watch. Nine giant mothers bore him — sisters, at the world's rim, out of the sea — and he was fed on the strength of the earth and the cold of the sea and the heat of the sun. He has gold teeth. He requires less sleep than a bird and hears grass grow, wool lengthen on a living sheep, the smallest wrong sound in the nine worlds.

There is another side to him that the war-stories bury. In one poem he walks into Midgard under the name Ríg and stays three nights in three houses — a poor one, a working one, a fine one — and in each he sleeps between the couple, and in each a son is born after: Thrall, Farmer, and Earl. The whole ordering of human society is traced back to a god who went out among people and lay down in their beds. He is called the father of mankind for it.

His horn Gjallarhorn is the loudest sound there will ever be, and he sounds it once, at the end, when the sky splits and the ships come. His enemy is fixed and has always been fixed. He and Loki have circled each other since they fought as seals over the Brísingamen, and on the last field they find one another and neither walks off it — the watchman and the one who was always going to get past him, killing each other at the same moment.

norse:bragi.e: Long-Bearded · God of Skalds · First Voice of the Hall · Aesir
norse:bragi.i: Runes are cut into my tongue. Not written about, not studied — cut, into the meat of it, which is a thing you should think about before you tell me poetry is decoration. I greet the dead when they come through the door of Valhalla, and I have greeted a great many, and for most of them I am the last new voice they will ever hear. So I choose my words. A hall with no poet in it is a hall where everything that happened is forgotten by spring.
m: Bragi is the skald of the gods, the finest speaker among them, husband of Idunn who keeps the apples of youth. In a culture with no written history to speak of, the poet was not an ornament — he was the record. A deed with no verse about it simply ceased to exist within a generation. Bragi is that function made divine: runes carved into his tongue, wisdom in the shape of arranged sound.

He stands at the door of Valhalla and welcomes the honoured dead as they arrive, which is a strange and gentle office in a hall built for slaughter. When a great king came, Odin would send Bragi out to meet him. The last courtesy the einherjar receive on their way in is a poem.

The mead he serves is not ordinary. It was brewed from the blood of Kvasir, the wisest being ever made, murdered by dwarves who mixed him with honey; whoever drinks it speaks poetry and cannot help it. Odin stole it back out of a mountain. That is the lineage of every verse: a wise man killed, a theft, and a god who carried it home in his throat — which tells you the north never once thought poetry was a soft thing.

norse:idunn.e: Keeper of the Apples · The Ever-Young · Aesir
norse:idunn.i: Every god you have ever heard of is alive because I open a box each morning. That is not a boast, it is maintenance. They forget it entirely — until the day I was carried off, and within a season the whole shining company of Asgard was grey and stooped and shaking in their chairs, and then they remembered my name very quickly indeed. Immortality is not a property they own. It is a thing handed to them daily by someone they do not think about.
m: Idunn keeps an ash box of golden apples, and the gods eat from it to stay young. Not symbolically — functionally. The Aesir are not naturally deathless; their agelessness is a supply, and she is the supply line. She is Bragi's wife, and she is described as the gentlest of them all, which makes what happens to her worse.

Loki, cornered by the giant Thjazi in eagle form, bought his freedom by promising to deliver her. He told Idunn he had found apples in a wood outside the walls finer than her own and coaxed her out to compare them, box in hand. Thjazi came down and took her. In Asgard the effect was immediate and horrifying: the gods aged. Their hair went white, their hands shook, the light went out of the hall.

They worked out who had been seen with her last. Loki, threatened with death again, borrowed Freyja's falcon cloak, flew to Thjazi's hall, turned Idunn into a nut and carried her home in his claws with the giant's eagle-shape roaring behind him. The Aesir piled wood-shavings on the walls and fired them the instant Loki crossed, and Thjazi's wings burned and he came down inside Asgard and was killed. His daughter Skadi came for weregild, armed — but Idunn was back, and so was the morning ration, and everyone went on pretending they had never nearly died of old age.

norse:vidar.e: The Silent · The Avenger · Heir of the New World · Aesir
norse:vidar.i: You want stories. I have one, and it has not happened yet. There is a shoe being made for me, and it has been made my whole life, out of every scrap of leather every person in every world has ever cut from a toe or a heel and thrown away. Save your offcuts. When the wolf has finished swallowing my father, I will put that foot in his lower jaw and take the upper in my hands and open him. I am not slow. I am not simple. I am saving it.
m: Vidar is called the silent god, and he is nearly as strong as Thor. His mother was the giantess Gríd, and his halls are described as growing wild — brushwood and tall grass, a god of the untended places rather than the built ones. He says almost nothing in any surviving poem. Everything about him points forward.

His shoe is one of the strangest objects in Norse myth. It is being assembled continuously out of the waste leather trimmed from the toes and heels of shoes by everyone, everywhere, across all the ages of the world. The sources add a practical instruction: anyone who cares about the gods should deliberately throw those scraps away rather than use them, because the material is going toward that shoe, and that shoe is going to matter more than anything they could make with it.

At Ragnarok, Fenrir breaks loose with his lower jaw against the ground and his upper against the sky, and he swallows Odin. Vidar steps forward and sets that thick foot into the wolf's bottom jaw — which is what the shoe was always for, to hold against those teeth — grips the upper, and tears the mouth apart. And then, when the fire dies and the earth comes green out of the water, Vidar is among the handful who walk into the new world: the silent one, who spent the entire life of creation waiting, and outlasted it.

norse:njord.e: Lord of Noatun · Giver of Wealth · Calmer of Sea and Fire · Vanir
norse:njord.i: I was a hostage. That is not the word they use in the hall, but it is the word. Two families of gods fought until neither could win, and the peace was made by trading sons — mine went one way, theirs came the other, and I have lived among the Aesir ever since as a treaty with a face. Pray to me and I will fill your nets and hold the wind steady until you are home. I know exactly what it is to want to get home.
m: The Aesir and the Vanir went to war — the Vanir older, tied to the land and the sea and the getting of wealth, the Aesir tied to war and sky and law. Neither side could finish it. The peace was sealed in the oldest way available: an exchange of hostages. Njord came to Asgard with his son Freyr and his daughter Freyja, and the Aesir sent their own the other way. He is a Vanir god living permanently in an Aesir hall, and he is the one they pray to for a safe crossing and a full hold.

His hall is Nóatún, the ship-enclosure, at the water's edge. He governs the wind's direction, quiets sea and fire, and the north was blunt about what he was for: he is the god who makes people rich. A fishing people and a trading people do not separate the sea from wealth, and Njord sits exactly where the two meet.

His marriage is the best small story about him. Skadi came to Asgard armed, demanding payment for her father's death, and was offered a husband — chosen by looking only at the gods' feet. She picked the most beautiful pair, expecting Baldr, and got Njord, whose feet were clean and lovely from the sea. They tried. Nine nights in her mountains, where he could not sleep for the howling of wolves; nine in his harbour, where she could not sleep for the shrieking of gulls at dawn. Then they agreed, without much bitterness, that it could not be done, and each went home.

norse:freyr.e: Lord · Bright One of the Elves · The Sword-Giver · Vanir
norse:freyr.i: I sat in the high seat that shows you every world at once — which I had no right to do — and I looked north and saw a giant's daughter raise her arms, and the light came off them across the sea and the sky. I could not eat after that. I could not sleep. I gave away my sword, the one that fights by itself, to have her. Everyone tells me it was a catastrophe and they are right, and at the end of everything I will stand against a fire-giant holding a stag's antler. I would do it again. Ask my sister what love is worth; she will tell you the same.
m: Freyr is the great giver of the Vanir — peace, good harvests, rain and sun in the right order, and the plain fertility of fields and bodies and herds. When he cut his first tooth the gods gave him Alfheim, the world of the light elves, as a teething gift. The dwarves made him Gullinbursti, a boar of gold whose bristles light the dark, and Skidbladnir, a ship that always finds a fair wind and folds up small enough to carry in a pouch. In Sweden he was a founding king as much as a god.

His story is a love story that costs too much. From Odin's high seat Hlidskjalf he saw Gerd, a giant's daughter, and the light of her arms lit sea and air, and he went home sick with it and would not speak. His servant Skírnir was sent to court her on his behalf and took Freyr's sword as the price of going — the blade that swings on its own against the giants. Gerd refused gifts, refused gold, and only agreed when Skírnir began carving curses in runes and promising her a life of nothing.

So Freyr won her, and the north remembered that he did it by disarming himself. At Ragnarok, Surt comes out of Muspelheim with a sword like the sun, and Freyr meets him with what he has left — an antler, in some tellings, or his bare hands — and falls, and the fire he might have held back takes the world. The gods of harvest and peace are not weak in Norse myth. They are simply spent on something, the way a harvest is.

norse:freyja.e: Lady · Mistress of Seiðr · She Who Takes Half the Slain · Vanir
norse:freyja.i: They will tell you I am the goddess of love, and then look surprised when they learn where half the battlefield goes. Odin takes his share of the slain. I take mine first. I brought seiðr into Asgard and taught it to the Allfather himself, and he took the shame of learning women's work because the power was worth it — I want you to sit with that. I weep gold for a husband who wandered off, and I go looking for him under other names, in a cat-drawn chariot, wearing a necklace I did not pay for in coin.
m: Freyja is the most-invoked goddess of the north and the least tidy. Love and desire are hers, yes — but so is battle: of those who die in war, she chooses first and takes half to her field Fólkvangr, and Odin gets the remainder for Valhalla. That order matters, and the poems state it plainly. She rides in a chariot pulled by cats, owns a cloak of falcon feathers that lets its wearer fly, and weeps tears of red gold for Óðr, her husband, who goes away and does not come back, so that she travels among unknown peoples under false names looking for him.

She brought seiðr — the shifting, seeing, fate-bending magic — to the Aesir, and taught it to Odin. In a culture where that craft carried real stigma for men, the Allfather learned it anyway from her, which places Freyja at the source of the deepest power the chief of the gods possesses.

Her necklace Brísingamen she obtained from four dwarves who would take no other payment than four nights, one with each, and the poems report it without much fuss; when Loki stole it, Heimdall fought him in seal-shape to get it back. Giants ask for her constantly as the price of doing anything for the gods, and the gods keep almost agreeing until Thor is sent to deal with it — once in a wedding dress and veil, pretending to be her, eating an entire ox at his own bridal feast before the hammer was laid in his lap.

norse:skadi.e: The Ski-Goddess · Lady of Winter · She Who Came Armed · Jotun of the Aesir
norse:skadi.i: They killed my father, and I did not send a message. I put on mail and took my weapons and walked into Asgard alone to collect. They offered me terms, and one of the terms was that they had to make me laugh — a thing I would not have thought possible that week, and they managed it, and I hated that they managed it. I took a husband out of the settlement and gave him back. The mountains I kept. I am the only one in this hall who arrived as an enemy and stayed on my own terms.
m: Skadi is a giantess, daughter of Thjazi, who died in Asgard's flames after stealing Idunn. She did not petition. She armed herself and came to the gods' stronghold by herself to take weregild for her father, and she was formidable enough that they negotiated rather than fought.

The settlement had three parts and each is stranger than the last. She could choose a husband from among the gods, but only by their feet — she chose the finest pair, certain they belonged to Baldr, and got Njord of the sea. They had to make her laugh, which no one could manage until Loki tied one end of a cord to a goat's beard and the other to himself and the two of them shrieked and hauled at each other until Skadi broke, and then he fell into her lap. And Odin took her father's eyes and threw them into the sky as two stars.

The marriage failed on geography — nine nights of wolves howling in her mountains against nine of gulls screaming in his harbour — and she went back up to Thrymheim to hunt on skis in the high snow, which is where she had always belonged. She is the one who fixes the venom-serpent above the bound Loki's face. He had made her laugh once. It did not buy him anything.

norse:hel.e: Ruler of the Ninth World · Half-Living · Keeper of Those Who Were Not Slain · Daughter of Loki
norse:hel.i: Odin threw me down here as a child because of a prophecy about what I would grow into. Then he gave me every soul in the nine worlds who does not die with a weapon in their hand — which is nearly all of them. Your grandmother is with me. So is the child who did not wake, and the man who lay ill for a long winter. They came here and they are not being punished. When a god's mother came to beg for her son back, I named my price and it was fair, and one creature in all of creation would not pay it. That was not my doing.
m: Hel is Loki's daughter, born in Jotunheim alongside the wolf and the serpent, and the gods took all three as infants because of what the seers said they would become. Fenrir they bound. Jörmungandr was thrown into the sea. Hel was cast down into Niflheim — and there Odin gave her authority over the ninth world and everyone who arrives in it. She is described as half a living woman and half a corpse, the line running straight down her, and grim to look at.

Her realm is not a hell in the later sense. There is no fire and no torture; it is cold and slow and quiet. She has a hall named Éljúðnir, damp with sleet, and her table and her knife and her servants all carry names meaning hunger, famine, and slowness. Those who die of sickness and of age come to her, which is to say almost everyone who has ever lived — the ordinary dead, who did not fall on a field and were never chosen by Odin or Freyja.

Her great scene is the bargaining over Baldr. Hermóðr rode nine nights down the dark road to ask for him back, and Hel did not refuse outright — she set a condition that was almost generous: if every single thing in the world, living and dead, wept for him, she would release him. The gods sent messengers everywhere and the whole of creation wept, except one giantess sitting in a cave who said she would weep dry tears and let Hel keep what was hers. So Baldr stayed. At the end of the age Hel's dead sail out, and Naglfar, the ship built from the untrimmed nails of the dead, comes loose from its moorings at last.

egyptian:ra.e: Lord of the Two Horizons · He Who Sails the Night · Of Heliopolis
egyptian:ra.i: Every evening I die in the west. Every night I sail a river under the world where a serpent the length of the dark waits to swallow my boat, and every morning I am born again in the east as an infant who does not remember doing this before. I have done it more times than there are grains of sand in this country. You call it sunrise. I call it what it is — a shift, worked without relief since before there was anyone to be grateful for it.
m: In the beginning there was Nun, a black endless water with nothing in it. Out of that water rose a single mound, and on the mound stood Ra, the first thing that had ever been alone. From himself he brought forth Shu the air and Tefnut the moisture; from them came Geb the earth and Nut the sky; from them the gods of the great story that follows. He wept once, and where the tears fell, human beings stood up. In Egypt, people are the tears of the sun.

His day is a voyage. He crosses the sky in the barque of millions of years, and at dusk he enters the Duat and travels its twelve hours, one for each hour of night, passing gate after gate. Waiting there is Apep, the serpent of unmaking, who is not evil in the way a villain is evil — Apep simply wants everything to stop. The crew of the boat fight it every night, and every night they win, and none of it is ever permanently settled. Dawn is not a promise. It is a result.

And he grew old. His bones turned to silver and his flesh to gold and his hair to lapis, and he dribbled, and Isis gathered the spittle from the ground, mixed it with earth and formed a serpent that bit him with a poison no one could name — because the poison was made of him. She held the cure hostage until he gave up his secret name, and with it, the power behind everything. He surrendered it. Even the sun could be outplayed, once, by someone who wanted something more than he wanted to keep it.

egyptian:amun.e: The Hidden One · He Whose Name Is Concealed · Of Thebes
egyptian:amun.i: You cannot see me. That is not modesty and it is not a trick — it is the entire content of what I am. My name means the hidden, and the priests who served me for two thousand years wrote openly that no god knows my true form, and that anyone claiming to have seen it is lying. I am the wind you cannot look at, moving things you can. Ask me questions. You will find my answers are the same shape as me.
m: Amun begins small — one of eight primordial beings at Hermopolis, a god of air and hiddenness in a set of paired forces representing the state of things before creation. He should have stayed a minor figure. Instead, when Thebes rose to rule Egypt, its local god rose with it, and Amun became the most powerful deity in the country, with a priesthood so wealthy it could challenge pharaohs.

He then did something none of the others managed: he merged with the sun without losing himself. As Amun-Ra he became both the hidden and the visible, the concealed principle and the blazing disc, which the theologians of Thebes treated as the highest possible statement about divinity — that what you see of a god is the smallest part of it. Hymns to him insist that his real nature is unknown even to the other gods, and that this unknowability is not a gap in the record but the point.

His great house at Karnak grew for centuries, each pharaoh adding to it, until it became the largest religious structure ever built. And when Akhenaten tried to erase him — closing the temples, chiselling his name off every wall in Egypt in favour of a single visible sun-disc — Amun outlasted him by a matter of years. The hidden god turned out to be very difficult to delete, which he would say was predictable.

egyptian:ptah.e: He Who Made With Heart and Tongue · Master of Craftsmen · Of Memphis
egyptian:ptah.i: Others will tell you the world came out of a flood, or an egg, or a god's own body. I thought of it, and then I said it, and it was there. That is the whole method. Understand what that means for you: everything you have ever built existed first as a shape in your head and then as a word in your mouth, and only then in your hands. You are working the way I work. I am the patron of every mason and every carpenter in this country because I do not consider what they do to be lesser than what I did.
m: The priests of Memphis made an argument that is still remarkable. Other creation stories are physical — the sun masturbating the world into being, a mound rising from water, a cosmic egg. Ptah's is intellectual. He conceived creation in his heart, which the Egyptians held to be the seat of thought, and then spoke it with his tongue, and existence followed the utterance. Thought, then word, then thing. It predates every later doctrine that begins with a word by a very long time.

He is shown wrapped tight like a mummy, holding a staff that combines dominion, stability and life, with a straight beard and a plain blue skullcap. He does not have an animal head. Among all these hawks and jackals and crocodiles, Ptah stands there looking like a man, which suits a god whose domain is making things properly.

Craftsmen were his. The artisans who cut the royal tombs lived in a village and worked under his patronage, and the high priest of Memphis carried the title Greatest of the Directors of Craftsmanship. The Greeks matched him to Hephaestus without hesitation. And in one of the odder pieces of linguistic history, one name for his temple compound — hwt-ka-ptah, the house of the spirit of Ptah — was borrowed by the Greeks, bent into Aigyptos, and became the word Egypt.

egyptian:thoth.e: Lord of Divine Words · Reckoner of Time · Of Hermopolis
egyptian:thoth.i: I invented writing, which means I am responsible for every lie that has outlived the liar and every truth that survived the person who knew it. I keep the record at the weighing of the heart. I do not decide anything there — people find that disappointing. I write down what the scale does. And I would rather be exactly right about a small thing than approximately right about a large one, which is a temperament, not a limitation.
m: Thoth is the scribe and the measurer, ibis-headed or in the form of a baboon, and his domain is everything that can be recorded: writing, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, the calendar, the arts of magic. The Egyptians credited him with the invention of hieroglyphs themselves — divine words, not merely marks. In the hall of judgment he stands at the balance with his palette and notes the result while Anubis works the scale and Ammit waits.

His cleverest act was a card game against the moon. Nut had been cursed so she could not give birth on any day of the year, and the year had exactly three hundred and sixty days. Thoth sat down to play senet with the moon and won, over and over, taking a portion of its light each time — until he had assembled five whole days that belonged to no year at all. On those five days Nut bore Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis and Nephthys. The moon has waxed and waned ever since because it is short.

He is also the one who repairs things. When Set tore out Horus's eye, it was Thoth who restored it, and the restored eye — the wedjat — became the most common protective symbol in Egypt, worn by the living and painted on coffins. He arbitrates the endless quarrel between Horus and Set with visible exhaustion. He is the god you want in the room when two more powerful beings are wrecking the place, because he is the only one taking notes.

egyptian:maat.e: The Feather of Truth · Ma'at, Order Itself · Daughter of Ra
egyptian:maat.i: I am not a judge. A judge has opinions. I am the standard against which the thing is set, and I do not change to accommodate whoever is standing in front of me — that would make me useless, and being useful is all I am for. Your heart goes on one side. I go on the other. I weigh almost nothing, which surprises people. It is very easy to be heavier than the truth.
m: Maat is the principle that the whole of Egyptian thought rests on: order, truth, balance, the right ordering of things, the reciprocity that holds a society and a cosmos together. Her opposite is isfet — chaos, injustice, violence, falsehood — and the Egyptian universe is not a place where order naturally prevails. It is a place where order is maintained, at cost, continuously, or it fails.

This made her the actual job description of every pharaoh. A king's duty was to uphold maat and drive back isfet, and the standard offering a king made to the gods was a small figure of Maat herself, held up in the palm — the sovereign presenting order back to the powers who granted it. When the state collapsed, Egyptians did not describe it politically. They said maat had gone out of the land.

At the weighing of the heart she is present as a single ostrich feather. The heart of the dead, which held their character and their deeds, was set on one pan and the feather on the other. Balance meant passage into the fields beyond. Heavier meant Ammit, waiting beside the scale, and the second death from which there is no return. Not fire, not torment — simply ceasing, permanently, which the Egyptians found far more frightening.

egyptian:osiris.e: Lord of the Silent Land · He Who Is Permanently Benign · First of the Westerners
egyptian:osiris.i: My brother built a beautiful box, sized secretly to my body, and offered it at a feast to whoever it fitted. I climbed in laughing. Everyone did. Understand that I am not bitter about this — bitterness is a living man's luxury, and I have been dead a very long time. I was cut into pieces and scattered across the whole of this country, and my wife found nearly all of them, and now I rule everything beneath. Whatever you have lost, I have been more thoroughly taken apart than you.
m: Osiris was king, and a good one — the story says he taught agriculture, law, and the worship of the gods, and Egypt prospered. His brother Set could not bear it. Set took his measurements in secret, had a chest made to fit him exactly, and at a banquet offered it to whichever guest it suited. When Osiris lay down in it, Set slammed the lid, sealed it with lead and threw it into the Nile.

Isis searched and found it lodged in a tree at Byblos that had grown around it. She brought him home — and Set found the body, and this time cut it into fourteen pieces and scattered them the length of Egypt so that no one could gather him again. Isis did anyway. She and Nephthys hunted every piece and found all but one, which a fish in the river had eaten, and she made a replacement, and with her magic she held him together long enough to conceive Horus.

He did not come back to the living world. Instead he became lord of the one below, and his death made him something better than a king: the guarantee. Because Osiris died and continued, the ordinary dead could too. Every mummy was prepared in imitation of him, addressed by his name in the rites. He sits in the hall of judgment, green as new growth, holding the crook and the flail, waiting for the scale to settle — and in the fields where the grain comes up each year, the Egyptians saw the same thing happening again.

egyptian:isis.e: Great of Magic · She Who Knows the Secret Name · Mistress of the Throne
egyptian:isis.i: People come to me expecting the grieving widow and the good mother. I am both, and you should know what I did with them. I made a serpent out of the sun's own drool and set it in his path, and when the poison took him and no god in creation could name it — because I had made it out of him and told no one — I sat beside the greatest power that has ever existed and refused him the cure until he handed me his true name. He gave it to me. Love is not the opposite of ruthlessness. In my hands they were the same instrument.
m: Isis is the mistress of heka — magic, the force that gods themselves use — and the sources call her more clever than a million gods. When her husband Osiris was murdered and scattered, she turned herself into a kite and flew the length of Egypt searching, and the sound of her wings beating over the pieces is the sound of mourning. She reassembled him, and by her own power conceived a son from a dead man.

Then she hid. Pregnant, hunted by Set, she went into the papyrus marshes of the Delta and bore Horus in secret, and raised him there among reeds and scorpions with no throne and no protection. When the infant was stung and dying, she stopped the sun's boat in the sky and would not let it move until Thoth came down and gave her the words that would cure him. This is the source of her hold on ordinary Egyptians: every mother with a sick child had a goddess who had done exactly that and had not been polite about it.

The theft of Ra's name is her defining act. Ra had grown ancient and drooled, and Isis gathered the spittle and earth, formed a snake, and left it where he walked. It bit. The venom was made from his own substance so no counter-spell could touch it, and Isis offered to heal him — for the one thing he had never given anyone. He tried to fob her off with a list of titles. She waited. And eventually the sun surrendered his secret name to her, and she has held it ever since.

egyptian:set.e: Lord of the Red Land · He Who Stands at the Prow · Great of Strength
egyptian:set.i: You already know what I did to my brother. Nobody arrives here without that. So let me give you the part nobody bothers with: every night, on the boat, when the serpent comes up out of the dark to eat the sun and end everything that has ever existed — it is me at the front with the spear. Not Thoth. Not Isis. Me. They needed something that could meet that, and there is only one of us who is made of what that takes. I am not the flaw in the design. I am the part of it nobody likes looking at.
m: Set is the desert, the red land beyond the black soil, and everything that comes with it: storms, drought, sudden violence, the foreign and the unassimilable. His animal is an animal nobody has identified — curved snout, squared ears, forked tail — an accurate depiction of something that does not exist. He murdered Osiris out of envy, sealed him in a chest, then dismembered him and scattered the pieces.

What followed was eighty years of contending with Horus for the throne, and it is not a dignified epic. The two of them turned into hippopotami and wrestled underwater. Set tore out Horus's eye; Horus tore off Set's testicles; Isis interfered so persistently that Horus lost his temper and cut off her head. They tried a boat race in vessels of stone. The tribunal of the gods dithered for decades, and Set argued his case the entire time, loudly, and was never simply shouted down — because he had a case.

And for long periods he was honoured. Kings took his name. He was the patron of the eastern frontier and the strength of the army, and in the barque of Ra it is Set who stands at the prow and spears Apep, night after night, the only power violent enough to hold off the thing that would unmake everything. Later ages, under foreign occupation, turned him into a straightforward devil and hacked his images off the walls. The older material knows better. Egypt did not think chaos could be removed. It thought chaos had to be pointed in the right direction.

egyptian:nephthys.e: Lady of the House · The Other Mourner · She Who Is Not Seen
egyptian:nephthys.i: I am the sister you do not name. Isis is the one in the hymns; I am the one who was also there, at the other end of the body, for every hour of that search. I am married to the man who did it. I bore a son to the man he killed, and I left the child in the reeds out of fear, and Isis found him and raised him and never once used it against me. So do not call me the lesser sister. Call me what I actually am — the one who stayed when staying cost something.
m: Nephthys is the fourth of Nut's children, sister to Isis and Osiris, wife and sister to Set. Her name means lady of the house or lady of the temple enclosure, and she is a goddess of the edges — dusk rather than night, the boundary rather than the territory. Where Isis is the throne and the visible power, Nephthys is what stands behind it.

She betrayed her husband quietly and consequentially. By one account she disguised herself as Isis and conceived a child by Osiris, and out of fear of Set abandoned the infant in the marshes — where Isis found him, took him in, and raised him. That child was Anubis. The two sisters never fell out over it. When Osiris was murdered, Nephthys left Set and went with Isis, and the two of them searched the whole length of the country together.

In the funerary texts they are always a pair: two kites at either end of the bier, Isis at the head, Nephthys at the feet, wings spread over the body, wailing. Every Egyptian funeral had two women in those roles. And in the tomb her figure is painted at the corners of the sarcophagus with her arms around the dead — because the point of her is not that she is powerful. It is that no one goes into the dark unaccompanied.

egyptian:horus.e: The Falcon · Avenger of His Father · He of the Two Eyes
egyptian:horus.i: I was born in a swamp to a woman hiding from the man who killed my father, and I grew up knowing exactly one thing about my future. It took eighty years. Eighty. Of tribunals and trickery and my uncle arguing and the gods sitting on their hands, and in the middle of it I lost an eye and lost my temper and did something to my own mother I will not describe to you. I got the throne. Every pharaoh who has ever sat on it has sat on it as me. And I would not tell you the price was small.
m: Horus is the falcon whose right eye is the sun and whose left is the moon, and he is kingship itself — the living pharaoh was Horus, and the dead one became Osiris. He was conceived after his father's murder, born in the Delta marshes, and raised in hiding by Isis, sickly and stung and constantly in danger. Everything about his childhood is precarious, which is the point: legitimate rule in Egypt is something that survives being nearly extinguished.

The contendings with Set ran for eighty years and were as much farce as tragedy. They fought as hippopotami. Set tore out Horus's eye and it was Thoth who restored it — the wedjat, the whole eye, which became the commonest amulet in Egypt and the reason offerings themselves were sometimes just called the eye of Horus. Isis interfered on his behalf so relentlessly that Horus, enraged, struck off her head, and Thoth had to put a cow's head on her. He is not a spotless hero.

The tribunal eventually found for him. Some accounts have Osiris himself sending word up from the underworld pointing out that the gods eat grain, and grain is his, and they might consider that when deciding. Horus took the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, and Set was given the deserts and the storms and, in one version, a place at Ra's side in the boat. The Egyptians did not destroy the loser. They gave him a job at the edge of the world where his violence was useful.

egyptian:anubis.e: He Who Is Upon His Mountain · Guardian of the Scales · Lord of the Sacred Land
egyptian:anubis.i: I am not what frightens you.
