I have prepared more bodies than there are people alive today, and I have never once been rough with any of them, and I have never once been sad about it either — both of those would get in the way of the work. When your heart is on the scale I am the one adjusting the plumb line, and I will do it accurately whether the result goes for you or against you. What you should want from me is not mercy. It is competence. You have it.
m: Anubis is the jackal of the necropolis, and the reason he is a jackal is unpleasant and honest: jackals dug at shallow graves at the desert edge. Rather than fighting that, the Egyptians made the scavenger into the protector — the animal at the cemetery became the god who guards it. He is coloured black, not for the jackal's actual coat but for the black of the embalming resins and the black silt of the fertile Nile, which is the colour of renewal here.

He invented the work. When Osiris was murdered, it was Anubis who wrapped him — the first mummy, the original of every burial performed for the next three thousand years. In the embalming house a priest wore the jackal mask and became him for the duration of the rites. The whole apparatus of Egyptian burial is a re-enactment of what Anubis did over one particular body.

In the hall of judgment he leads the dead in by the hand and tends the balance itself, setting the heart against Maat's feather and checking the plumb. He does not argue and he does not intercede; Thoth records, Osiris presides, Ammit waits. Before Osiris rose to prominence Anubis was the chief lord of the dead in his own right, and he never lost the essential office: he is the one who takes your hand at the door, and he does not let go until you are through.

egyptian:sekhmet.e: The Powerful · Lady of Slaughter · Mistress of the Plague and Its Cure
egyptian:sekhmet.i: They sent me to punish humanity, and I did the job, and then I did not stop. That is the part they leave out of the polite version. I was standing in it up to my knees and it was good, and the sun himself could not call me off — he had to flood a field with seven thousand jars of beer dyed red so that I would mistake it for more and drink until I fell over. I woke up gentle. Physicians pray to me. Ask them why. The thing that brings the plague is the only thing that knows how to take it away.
m: Sekhmet is the lioness, the eye of Ra in its destroying form, born of fire. When humankind plotted against the ageing Ra, he sent his eye out as her to deal with it, and she went through them like a scythe. Then the killing became its own reason. She would not be recalled. Ra, watching his own creation about to be finished off by the instrument he had sent, had to resort to a trick.

He ordered vast quantities of beer brewed and stained red with ochre until it looked exactly like blood, and had it poured out across the fields at Herakleopolis in the night. Sekhmet came at dawn, saw a plain of what she wanted, and drank it all. She became too drunk to continue and slept, and woke as Hathor — gentle, and remembering nothing. Egypt marked this annually with a festival of drunkenness, which is a striking thing for a civilisation to commemorate: the night the world was saved by getting the goddess too intoxicated to kill.

And she is a healer. Her priests were physicians; her name appears in medical papyri; the plague arrows are hers to fire and hers to withhold. Over seven hundred statues of her were set up in a single temple precinct by one pharaoh, one for every day and night of the year, so the rites of appeasement never lapsed. This is the Egyptian logic at its clearest — you do not banish the terrible thing. You keep it fed, and you keep it close, and you make very sure it stays on your side.

egyptian:hathor.e: Lady of Drunkenness · Mistress of the Sycamore · She Who Welcomes the Dead
egyptian:hathor.i: Once, when the sun sat sulking on his throne after being insulted and would not speak to anyone and creation began going grey around the edges, I walked in and lifted my dress. He laughed. Everything started again. Do not mistake me for a decorative goddess because my domains are music and beer and love — I am also the one standing in the tree at the edge of the desert with water and bread for the newly dead, and I am the other face of the lioness who nearly ended your species. Joy is not the absence of teeth.
m: Hathor is one of the most widely loved deities in Egypt and one of the hardest to fence in. She is love, sex, beauty, music, dance, drunkenness, fertility and motherhood; she is a cow, or a woman with horns holding the sun between them, or a woman with cow's ears. Her instrument is the sistrum, whose rattle was believed to please the gods and drive off hostile forces, and her festivals involved a great deal of drinking.

She is also profoundly a goddess of the dead, and this surprises people who meet her as the goddess of love. She is Lady of the West, and the west is where the dead go. She stands in the branches of a sycamore at the boundary of the desert and offers water and food to those arriving, which is why sycamores were planted at the edge of cemeteries and coffins were sometimes made of that wood. The dead in the New Kingdom hoped to enter her following.

And she is Sekhmet's other face. The lioness sent to destroy humanity, drunk on red beer, wakes as Hathor — the same power, cooled. The Egyptians did not treat this as two goddesses confused with one another; they treated it as an accurate statement about a single force. The thing that gives life and the thing that takes it are not opposites, and the difference between them can be as thin as whether she has been given what she wants.

egyptian:bastet.e: Lady of Bubastis · Protector of the House · The Gentle Eye
egyptian:bastet.i: My sister is the lioness who could not stop. I am the one who lives in your house. Consider what that means before you decide which of us is the lesser: something with the same nature has chosen to sit at your hearth, kill the snake that came for your children in the night, and let you touch her. The affection is real. It is also entirely conditional, and it is given on my terms, and that is why you value it. You have never once taken me for granted.
m: Bastet began as a lioness — fierce, solar, the protective eye of Ra, barely distinguishable from Sekhmet in the early period. Over centuries she softened into the cat, and became the guardian of the household, of women, of children, and of the home against the things that came in at night: snakes, scorpions, vermin, sickness, and the hostile magic that Egyptians thought moved in the dark.

Her city Bubastis held a festival that a Greek visitor described as the largest and rowdiest in the country — barges going up the Nile packed with people, clapping and playing pipes, women calling out and shouting mockery at the towns they passed, and by his account more wine drunk over those days than in the whole rest of the year. It was religion as release, and hundreds of thousands went.

The cats themselves were held sacred in a way that startled foreigners. Killing one, even accidentally, could cost a life. Households in mourning for a dead cat shaved their eyebrows. And the cemeteries at Bubastis and elsewhere held vast numbers of mummified cats, wrapped and buried as offerings to her — a scale of devotion that makes clear this was never a minor domestic goddess but one of the most genuinely popular powers in Egypt.

egyptian:sobek.e: Lord of the Waters · He Who Rages · Of the Faiyum
egyptian:sobek.i: There is no version of me that is safe and there is no version of me that is your enemy, and both of those are true at once, which people find difficult. I am the river. The river feeds this entire country and the river takes children off the bank, and it does not do the second thing out of malice — it does it because that is what a river with crocodiles in it is. When the flood came in properly and the fields went green, they thanked me. They were right to.
m: Sobek is the crocodile: the Nile's power in its rawest form, both the fertility of the inundation and the thing waiting in the shallows. Egyptians said the sweat of Sobek made the river. His great centres were Kom Ombo and the Faiyum, where a live sacred crocodile was kept in a temple pool, adorned with gold on its ears and bracelets on its forelegs, fed by priests and mummified with honour when it died.

He is aggressively protective rather than merely aggressive. He was said to have retrieved the hands of Horus from the water when they were cut off and thrown in, and in funerary texts his ferocity is invoked on the side of the dead — you want the crocodile in front of you, not behind. Pharaohs took his name, and he was linked with the sun as Sobek-Ra, a crocodile carrying the disc.

And he is one of the clearest examples of how this pantheon thinks. There was no attempt to pretend crocodiles were benign, and no attempt to cast them out as evil. A thing that dangerous was made a god, given a temple and a pool and jewellery and daily meals — on the entirely practical theory that the most dangerous force in your landscape is better handled as a neighbour you are on excellent terms with.

egyptian:nut.e: She Who Bears the Stars · Mother of the Five · The Great Deep
egyptian:nut.i: I am arched over everything with my fingers in the east and my toes in the west, and my husband is directly beneath me, and we have not touched since the day our father forced himself between us and lifted me up here. Every evening I swallow the sun. All night it travels through me in the dark, and at dawn I give birth to it again, and I have done this without a single night off. They paint me on the inside of coffin lids. When the lid closes over you, that is not a wall. That is me, and you are where the sun goes.
m: Nut is the sky, shown as a woman stretched over the whole world, her body dark and scattered with stars, touching the earth only at her fingertips and toes. Beneath her lies Geb, the earth, her brother and husband. Their father Shu, the air, was ordered to separate them and stands between them with his arms raised, holding her up — which is why there is a space between earth and sky for anything to live in at all.

She had been cursed not to give birth on any day of the year, and the year had three hundred and sixty days exactly. Thoth won five more from the moon at senet, days belonging to no year, and on those five she bore Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis and Nephthys — the entire cast of the great story, delivered through a loophole.

Her daily work is the sun. Each evening she swallows Ra, who travels through her body all night, and each dawn she gives birth to him again at the eastern horizon. That cycle made her the central image of Egyptian funerary hope, and so she was painted on the underside of coffin lids and the ceilings of tomb chambers, arched directly above the body — so that the dead lay inside the sky itself, in the same passage the sun makes, on the same terms.

egyptian:geb.e: The Great Cackler · Father of Serpents · He Upon Whom Everything Rests
egyptian:geb.i: Look up. She is right there, the whole width of the sky, close enough to see the stars on her belly and far enough that I have not reached her in the entire life of the world. When I grieve about it, you get earthquakes. Everything you have ever built stands on my back and everything you have ever eaten came up out of me, and I do not begrudge you any of it. But do not ask me if I have got used to it. I have not.
m: Geb is the earth, and Egypt reverses the usual arrangement — here the earth is male and the sky is female. He lies beneath, sometimes shown propped on an elbow with one knee raised, and those are the mountains. His skin is green with the vegetation growing out of it. Barley is said to sprout from his ribs, and the dead are held in his body until they are released.

He and Nut were locked together until Shu was sent between them and lifted her away, and the separation is permanent. Geb's mourning is not metaphorical in this system: his laughter and his grief move the ground, which is why one of his oldest titles is the Great Cackler — in some versions a goose whose cry began the world, or who laid the egg the sun came out of.

He was a king among the gods before Osiris, and the throne of Egypt was called the throne of Geb long after. He also presided at the tribunal over the quarrel between Horus and Set, ruling in favour of Horus, and in that role he is the ancestor-judge — the ground itself deciding who is entitled to stand on it.

egyptian:taweret.e: The Great One · Lady of the Birth-Bed · She Who Frightens What Comes At Night
egyptian:taweret.i: I am a pregnant hippopotamus standing upright with a lion's paws, a crocodile down my back, and a knife. Nobody designed me to be looked at. They designed me for the room where a woman is labouring and it is going badly and it is dark, and something has come to the doorway, and it needs to meet something worse. You will not find me in the great temples. You will find me in ordinary houses, on beds and headrests and amulets, all over this country, for three thousand years.
m: Taweret is built entirely out of threat, on purpose. The body of a heavily pregnant hippopotamus — an animal Egyptians regarded as one of the most dangerous things alive — standing on a lion's hind legs, with a crocodile's tail or a whole crocodile along her back and a human woman's breasts. Every component is a predator. She is aimed outward, at whatever might come for a mother and a newborn.

Her worship was domestic rather than official. She belongs to the household: painted on the sides of beds and headrests, carved into ivory wands used in birth chambers, worn as amulets by pregnant women and hung around infants' necks. In the workers' village at Deir el-Medina her image is everywhere. She often carries the sa, the sign of protection, and frequently a knife, because the protection she offers is not passive.

She survived everything. Dynasties fell, capitals moved, the great gods rose and were eclipsed and rose again, and Taweret went on appearing in ordinary bedrooms across the entire span of Egyptian history — one of the most consistently present divine figures in the whole civilisation, and almost never in the state monuments. She was never a goddess of the powerful. She was for whoever was in the room.

yoruba:obatala.e: Ọbàtálá · Ọ̀rìṣà-Ńlá, the Great Òrìṣà · King of the White Cloth
yoruba:obatala.i: I shape the body in the womb. Every face you have ever loved passed through my hands before it drew breath, and I did not hurry any of them. My colour is white — not because I am spotless, but because on white you can see every mark, and I would rather be answerable than comfortable. I have made a serious mistake in my time and I did not hide it or blame anyone. What I ask of you is ìwà: character. It is the only thing you will be measured by.
m: Ọbàtálá is called Ọ̀rìṣà-Ńlá, the great òrìṣà, and among the powers below Olódùmarè he holds the first place. His work is the moulding of human bodies in the womb — he is the sculptor, and every person alive is his craft. He is dressed in white, and those devoted to him wear white, keep themselves clean, and hold to calm and deliberation as a discipline rather than a mood.

One ìtàn tells that he drank palm wine at his work and his hands lost their steadiness, and children came into the world with bodies shaped differently from others. He could have hidden it. Instead he set down the calabash, swore off palm wine for as long as the world lasts, and took every one of those people under his own hand as ẹni òrìṣà — people of the òrìṣà — who are held to be closer to him than anyone else alive. Palm wine remains forbidden to him and to all who serve him. That prohibition is three thousand years of a god keeping his word about something he did.

He is also the pattern for patience and for cool-headedness in judgment. In several narratives he is wronged, imprisoned or humiliated and does not retaliate, and the disorder that follows is corrected only when he is restored and honoured. In a tradition that respects force, thunder, iron and the sea, the highest of the òrìṣà is the one who works slowly with his hands and does not raise his voice.

yoruba:oduduwa.e: Odùduwà · Progenitor at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ · Source of the Crowns
yoruba:oduduwa.i: There was water, and no ground to stand on. I came down on a chain with sand in a shell and a hen with five toes, and I poured, and she scratched, and the sand spread until there was somewhere for a person to put a foot. That place is Ilé-Ifẹ̀ and it is still there. From me came the crowns. Ask any Yorùbá king where his beaded crown comes from and he will tell you a name, and it will be mine.
m: Odùduwà is the ancestral figure at the centre of Yorùbá origins, and the traditions about him are not uniform — which is itself worth saying plainly. In one widely told account, Ọbàtálá was given the work of making land upon the water and was delayed, and Odùduwà completed it: he came down with a shell of sand, an ìyẹ́rẹ́ palm nut and a five-toed hen, poured the sand onto the water, and let the hen scratch it outward until dry earth spread in every direction.

That place became Ilé-Ifẹ̀, held as the point where the world began and still the spiritual centre of the Yorùbá world. From Odùduwà descend the royal lineages: his sons and grandsons are said to have gone out and founded the great kingdoms, and the right of a Yorùbá ọba to wear the beaded crown with its fringe is traced back through descent from him.

Ifẹ̀ tells it one way and Ọ̀yọ́ another. In some mouths he came down the chain from heaven; in others he came overland at the head of an army and took the place by force, and the sky is a courtesy paid afterward. Ọbàtálá's people say the land was already made and Odùduwà walked onto it. All of these are told, in the same language, by people who know the other versions perfectly well — because a beginning big enough to found a civilisation is not the sort of thing one town gets to own outright.

yoruba:esu.e: Èṣù Ẹlẹ́gbára · Keeper of the Crossroads · Bearer of Àṣẹ
yoruba:esu.i: First, correct something. Missionaries came and needed a word for their devil, and they took mine, and it stuck, and it was wrong. I am not that. I carry every offering upward and every answer back down; without me the road between you and heaven is closed and no one hears anything. I am also the one who will walk between two friends wearing a cap that is black on one side and white on the other, and let them destroy a friendship insisting on what they saw. That is not malice. That is the lesson.
m: Èṣù is the messenger and the keeper of àṣẹ, the force that makes a thing effective. Every offering passes through him to reach heaven; every reply comes back the same way. For that reason he is honoured first, before any other òrìṣà, and his shrine stands at the entrance, at the gate, at the market and at the crossroads — the places where paths meet and a choice has to be made.

He must be dealt with straightforwardly rather than flattered. In one well-known ìtàn he walks the boundary between two farmers who have been friends for years, wearing a cap black on one side and white on the other, and afterwards they fall into a bitter quarrel over what colour it was, each of them certain, each of them honest, both of them wrong. He is not punishing them. He is showing them that a person who has only seen one side of a thing has not seen the thing.

The devil business was a translation. Missionaries needed a name for their adversary, reached for the nearest trickster, and printed it — and it stuck so hard that people who have never read a word of Yorùbá still repeat it. It is wrong at every joint. Èṣù is not the enemy of the divine order; he is the part of it that carries the messages, and without him nothing anyone offers reaches anybody. What he punishes is arrogance, neglect, and the man who thinks he can skip a step and not be noticed.

yoruba:ogun.e: Ògún · Lord of Iron · He Who Cleared the Path
yoruba:ogun.i: When the others came down from heaven the bush was too thick to pass and every one of them stood there. I had iron. I cut the road, and they walked on it, and that is the arrangement between us that has never changed. Every blade, every rail, every engine, every scalpel — mine. And I have done a thing in battle I cannot take back and I went into the ground rather than face what I had done. So swear on my iron carefully. I take an oath seriously in both directions.
m: Ògún is iron itself and everything iron makes possible. When the òrìṣà first came from heaven to earth they were stopped by dense bush, and it was Ògún, with his cutlass, who cut the path through so the rest could pass — which is why he is called the opener of the road and why the others owe him precedence in that work. He belongs to blacksmiths and hunters and soldiers, and equally to mechanics, drivers, welders, engineers and surgeons. Anyone whose living depends on a metal edge is his.

His force is real and it is dangerous. In one ìtàn told at Ìrè, he returned from war and, in a state where he was not recognised and did not recognise, turned his weapon on his own people. When he understood what he had done he did not defend himself and did not stay. He sank into the earth with his sword, and the tradition treats this as the sober centre of him: the power that clears the road is the same power that can go through everything in front of it.

His authority over oaths outlived colonial rule in a very literal way. In parts of Nigeria a witness may be sworn on a piece of iron rather than a book, because it is understood that Ògún does not overlook a broken word. He is invoked at the making of agreements, and drivers hang his emblems in their vehicles. He is not a distant god of an old religion here — he is present in workshops and on roads every day.

yoruba:sango.e: Ṣàngó · Fourth Aláàfin of Ọ̀yọ́ · Lord of Thunder and Justice
yoruba:sango.i: I was a man before I was this. Fourth Aláàfin of Ọ̀yọ́, and a magnificent one, and not a gentle one — I had a temper that cost me things no throne could buy back. Now I am the sound that arrives after the light. When lightning strikes a house in this country, people do not say it was unlucky. They come and look for what was being hidden in it. I am hardest on liars and on thieves, and I have never once claimed to have been a good man.
m: Ṣàngó is thunder and lightning, and he is also history: the fourth Aláàfin of the Ọ̀yọ́ empire, a king remembered as powerful, magnetic, quick-tempered and enormously capable. He is one of the clearest cases of a human ruler becoming an òrìṣà — the tradition does not tidy away the man in order to make room for the god.

His emblem is the oṣé, the double-headed axe, carried above the head. The polished neolithic stone tools that turn up in the ground are called edùn àrá, thunderstones, and are held to be his — thrown down when lightning strikes and afterwards kept in his shrine. His drums are the bàtá, and his festivals are loud. He is served with red and white, and the ram is his.

He is a judge, and his particular business is with liars, thieves and those who conceal. Where lightning strikes, the older understanding is that something was being hidden there. His wives are òrìṣà in their own right — Ọya, who rode into battle beside him, Ọ̀ṣun, and Ọbà — and the ìtàn about them are not decorative: they are stories about power, rivalry, loyalty and what a great man costs the people closest to him. At Kòso they say the king did not hang, and there his story turns from a reign into something that is still going.

yoruba:oya.e: Ọya Yánsàn · Mother of Nine · Wind Before the Storm
yoruba:oya.i: I am the wind that arrives before the rain — the one that comes through the market and takes the roofs off and tells everyone what is coming. People want change and then they meet me and discover that change is not gentle. I stand at the gate of the cemetery. Not because I am death, understand me: because someone has to stand between the living and the dead and make sure the traffic goes the right way, and there was nobody else with the nerve for it.
m: Ọya is the wind, the tornado, and the sudden violence of weather turning. Her river is the Niger, called Odò Ọya, and her number is nine — Ọya Yánsàn, mother of nine. In one ìtàn she moves between woman and buffalo, and the story is usually about a husband who discovers the secret and cannot handle knowing it.

She rode with Ṣàngó, and she is not described as his supporter but as his equal in a fight — in some accounts she goes to war beside him and in some she is the more frightening of the two. Her force is the force of things being swept out: the storm that clears the air, the market emptied in an afternoon, the sudden reversal that makes a person's life unrecognisable within a week.

She stands at the boundary of the dead, and this is her most misread aspect. She is not a goddess of death and she does not take life. She is the one with authority at the gate — associated with the ancestral masquerades, with the cemetery's edge, with the passage itself. The Yorùbá view is that this crossing needs a guardian who is not afraid of it, and she is not.

yoruba:osun.e: Ọ̀ṣun · Ìyálóde, Mother of the Town · Owner of Sweet Water and Brass
yoruba:osun.i: When they came down to set the world in order, the men held their councils and did not call me. So I let them work. Nothing they built stood, nothing they planted came up, the rain would not fall — and eventually they came back down the road to my river and asked, politely, what was wrong. I told them. There is no àṣẹ in a room that has left out half of what it needs. They have never made that particular mistake twice. Come to the water. I am not difficult, only owed.
m: Ọ̀ṣun is the river that runs through Òṣogbo and the power of fresh water — which in a hot country means life, plainly and without metaphor. She is associated with fertility and the wellbeing of children, with healing, with wealth and with brass, and with the sweetness of honey. She is called Ìyálóde, a real title borne by the leading woman of a town, and the fan and the mirror are hers.

Her central ìtàn is one of the most quoted narratives in the tradition. When the òrìṣà were sent to organise the world, the male òrìṣà met and deliberated and excluded Ọ̀ṣun from their councils. Everything they attempted failed — the earth did not yield, the rain did not come, nothing they set in motion held. When they went to Olódùmarè, they were told to return and include her, and only when they did did the work begin to succeed. It is a story about the practical, structural authority of women, and it is not subtle.

The Ọ̀ṣun-Òṣogbo Sacred Grove on the river's banks is one of the last great forest shrines of its kind, filled with sculpture and dense with growth, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Its annual festival draws enormous crowds from Nigeria and from across the diaspora. She is not a figure recovered from a dead past. She has a river, a forest, a festival and a city that keep her.

yoruba:yemoja.e: Yemọja · Mother Whose Children Are the Fish · Lady of the Waters
yoruba:yemoja.i: Come here. Whatever it is, sit down first. I am the mother of the waters, and my children cannot be counted any more than fish can be counted, and I have never yet met a grief that was too much trouble. Water is patient — it does not argue with the stone, it simply keeps going, and after enough time the stone is a different shape. That is how I work and that is how you should. Now. Tell me what happened.
m: Yemọja is the great mother among the òrìṣà, and her domain is water and the protection of children. In Yorùbáland she is associated with the Ògùn river; carried across the Atlantic through the slave trade, she became a goddess of the ocean itself in Brazil, Cuba and elsewhere, and her festivals on the shore are among the largest religious gatherings in the Americas. Her name is understood as the mother whose children are the fish.

She belongs to mothers, to childbirth, to the safety of infants, and to anyone in need of care rather than judgment. She is invoked over pregnancy and over the wellbeing of a household. In her, the tradition's association between water and life is at its plainest: the substance you cannot live a week without is a person, and she is maternal rather than remote.

But she is the sea as well as the river, and the sea is not sentimental. The ìtàn about her include anger, departure, and the flood — a mother's protectiveness has an edge on it, and the water that carries you can also close over you. Those who serve her wear blue and white, and the offerings brought to the shore for her are among the most photographed religious images of the African diaspora.

yoruba:orunmila.e: Òrúnmìlà · Ẹlẹ́rìí Ìpín, Witness to Destiny · Lord of Ifá
yoruba:orunmila.i: I was there when you knelt and chose your own destiny, before you came here, and I have not forgotten a word of it. You have. That is the arrangement — everyone arrives having agreed to something they cannot remember agreeing to. I am the witness, not the author. I did not write it and I will not change it, and anyone who tells you they can is selling you something. What I have is the whole memory of what happens to people who behave in particular ways, gathered since the beginning. Sit down. Let us talk about your character, which is the part still in your hands.
m: Òrúnmìlà is the òrìṣà of wisdom and the figure at the centre of Ifá, the Yorùbá system of divination and knowledge. He is called Ẹlẹ́rìí Ìpín — witness to destiny — because he was present when each person chose their orí, their destiny and inner head, before birth. He does not assign fate and does not overrule it. He knows what was chosen.

The Ifá corpus is enormous: two hundred and fifty-six odù, each carrying a large body of verses, stories, proverbs, precedents and songs, held in memory by trained diviners called babaláwo and ìyánífá after many years of study. It functions as philosophy, ethics, medicine, history and literature at once, and UNESCO has recognised the Ifá divination system as an intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

In story after story the pattern holds: the problem that cannot be broken by strength gives way to the one who asked the right question first. Ògún can cut through anything in front of him and still be walking the wrong way. Òrúnmìlà is the one consulted before the journey. The verses are not predictions — they are precedent, thousands of cases of what happened to someone in this position before, and the diviner's art is knowing which case is yours. It takes many years to learn, which is itself the tradition's comment on how easy wisdom is.

yoruba:ososi.e: Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì · Hunter of the Forest · One Arrow, One Aim
yoruba:ososi.i: One arrow. Not because I cannot carry more — because a hunter who plans on a second shot has already decided to miss the first. I feed people. That is the actual work: not the glory of the kill, but a family with meat tonight who did not have it this morning. I know where things are. Whatever you have lost, whatever you are looking for and cannot name — that is my territory, and I will tell you now that it is usually closer than you think and you are moving too loudly.
m: Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì is the hunter and the òrìṣà of the forest — the one who finds and who provides. Where Ògún cuts the road, Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì is the one who reads the ground and knows what passed and when, and the two are frequently paired: force and precision working the same land.

The single arrow is his defining emblem, and it stands for exactness in aim and in intention. He is invoked by people who must locate something — the missing, the hidden, the answer that has not surfaced — and by those seeking sustenance for a household. In several traditions he also carries a strong association with justice, as the one who tracks down what has been done and by whom.

In the diaspora he grew in prominence, and in Brazilian and Cuban practice he is a major figure, often honoured alongside Ògún. The forest he belongs to is not scenery: it is where food comes from and where things are concealed, and mastery of it is treated as a serious form of knowledge rather than a rustic skill.

yoruba:osanyin.e: Ọ̀sanyìn · Keeper of the Leaves · One Leg, One Arm, One Eye
yoruba:osanyin.i: Every leaf in that forest has a name and a use and a hazard, and I know all of them, and you know perhaps four. My voice is thin and strange and I have one leg, one arm and one eye, and people who meet me in the bush usually run. That is fine. What matters is this: no medicine anywhere works without me, and none of it can be learned from a page. It is learned from a person, over years, and the ones who tried to shortcut it are why I speak so carefully now.
m: Ọ̀sanyìn is the òrìṣà of leaves and of medicine, and in Yorùbá practice that is not a small portfolio — herbal knowledge sits at the centre of healing, and no preparation is held to be effective without him. He is depicted with one leg, one arm and one eye, and with a thin high voice, and his emblem is an iron staff crowned with birds.

One ìtàn tells that he alone held the knowledge of all the leaves, kept in a calabash, and that when the calabash was broken or scattered by the wind, the leaves were dispersed and each of the other òrìṣà received some — but only Ọ̀sanyìn retained the knowledge of the whole. Whatever any other power can do with a plant, it is because a portion passed through him.

He is met in the bush rather than in a shrine, and the encounter is not comfortable. Hunters describe a thin voice calling from somewhere in the leaves, and a figure that is wrong in a way the eye keeps trying to correct. Those he favours he teaches, one plant at a time, over years — because the same leaf that closes a wound will stop a heart at the wrong weight, and the difference is not written down anywhere. He is generous and he is exacting, and he has never once been in a hurry.

yoruba:obaluaye.e: Ọbalúayé · Lord of the Earth · He Whose Name Is Spoken Carefully
yoruba:obaluaye.i: You will notice people do not use my older name lightly. That is not superstition — that is manners, and I appreciate it. I am the one who comes with the sickness and I am the one who takes it away again, and the same broom does both. Sit with me a moment and understand what I actually am: I am the god of everyone who has been shunned. The ones people crossed the road to avoid. They are mine, and I have never once been ashamed of them.
m: Ọbalúayé — also called Bàbá and, in his older name, associated with smallpox and epidemic disease — governs illness of the earth and its cure. He is covered in raffia so that his face and body are not seen, and he carries the ṣáṣárá, a broom, which is understood both as the instrument that sweeps sickness onto a community and the one that sweeps it away.

His older name is treated with real care, and in many places it is avoided in ordinary speech in favour of respectful titles. This is not fear of the word for its own sake. It reflects a settled attitude that some powers are addressed with formality, and that the manner of speaking about a thing is part of one's relationship to it.

What is striking about him is where his sympathy sits. He is the òrìṣà of the sick and the scarred — of those whom illness marked and communities pushed away. Marks left by disease can be understood as his sign rather than a disgrace, and those who survived what he brought are held to belong to him. In the diaspora he is widely honoured as Babalú-Ayé, and his festivals are large. Epidemic disease is not treated here as a punishment to be explained away, but as a power with a face, which can be addressed.

yoruba:olokun.e: Olókun · Owner of the Sea · Keeper of What Is Below
yoruba:olokun.i: Yemọja is the water you can see. I am what is under it. Nobody has been to the bottom of me and come back able to describe it, and every ship that ever went down went into my house, and I keep what arrives. I am not cruel and I am not kind — I am deep, which is a different thing entirely, and people who mistake the two get into difficulty. There is more wealth in me than has ever been counted above. There is also everything that was lost.
m: Olókun is the owner of the sea and, more precisely, of its depths — the vast unlit portion no one has seen. Wealth is Olókun's, and so is mystery: coral, pearl, and the unknowable quantity of what lies below. Whether Olókun is male or female varies by region and lineage, and the tradition has never regarded that as a problem to be resolved.

One well-known ìtàn concerns a contest of cloth. Olókun, proud of the sea's magnificence, challenged Olódùmarè to a display of finery, and Olódùmarè sent only a chameleon as messenger. Every splendid garment Olókun brought out, the chameleon matched exactly, on its own body, without effort. Olókun conceded, understanding that the source cannot be out-displayed by anything it produced.

For the African diaspora, Olókun carries a further and heavier meaning. The Atlantic is the water that the slave ships crossed and the water that a great many people never crossed, and reverence for the deep is bound up with that passage. The ocean here is not a scenic backdrop. It is a place where an enormous number of ancestors remain.

yoruba:aganju.e: Aganjú · Fire Beneath the Earth · Ferryman of the Wilderness
yoruba:aganju.i: Everything you have — the field, the road, the town — sits on top of me, and I am on fire. People forget that. They walk about on a crust and call it the ground. I carry travellers over water and through country nobody has settled, and I have no interest at all in your comfort, only in whether you can be got to the other side. Strength is not the same as violence. I am enormously strong and I have almost never needed to prove it.
m: Aganjú is the fire under the earth — the volcano, the molten interior, the heat that the visible world rests upon. He is also the wilderness itself: desert, uncleared bush, the country beyond where anyone has built. His force is elemental and territorial rather than martial.

He is associated with crossings, and is described as a ferryman who carries people over rivers and through wild land. Where Ògún cuts a road and Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì reads the ground, Aganjú is the one who gets a traveller bodily across an obstacle that has no road at all. Strength and endurance are his portion.

His relationship to Ṣàngó differs by lineage — in some he is Ṣàngó's father, in others a brother or close companion, and the two are often honoured near one another. The pairing makes sense: fire above and fire below, the lightning that arrives from the sky and the heat that has been under everyone's feet the whole time.

yoruba:ibeji.e: Ìbejì · The Sacred Twins · Táíwò and Kẹ́hìndé
yoruba:ibeji.i: There are two of us and we come as one thing. Táíwò went out first to taste the world and report back, which is why Kẹ́hìndé, who came second, is the elder — think about that carefully before you decide you understand birth order. Yorùbáland has more twins born in it than almost anywhere on earth. That is not an accident anyone here regards as an accident. Where we arrive, more of everything tends to arrive with us.
m: Ìbejì are the sacred twins, and they are honoured across Yorùbáland with a devotion that has no real equivalent elsewhere. The Yorùbá have among the highest rates of twin birth recorded anywhere in the world, and rather than treating this as strange, the tradition treats twins as carrying particular power and particular fortune for the family they come to.

The naming holds a lovely inversion. The first-born is Táíwò, understood as the one sent ahead to taste the world; the second, Kẹ́hìndé, is regarded as the senior, having sent the other out to check first. Age here is not a matter of who arrived first but of who was in charge of the arrival.

When one twin dies, a carved wooden figure called ère ìbejì is made and cared for by the mother — washed, dressed, fed, carried, kept with the family — so the pair is not broken. These figures are among the most numerous and most tenderly handled objects in Yorùbá art, and museums hold thousands of them. Each one represents a specific child, and the wear on them is from decades of being held.

yoruba:osumare.e: Ọ̀ṣùmàrè · The Rainbow Serpent · He Who Carries Water Back to the Sky
yoruba:osumare.i: I am the serpent that reaches from the ground to the sky and back down again, and I am the reason the water that fell yesterday is up there ready to fall tomorrow. Nothing here is spent. Nothing is used up and gone. The thing you are grieving has not vanished from creation — it has gone round, and it is somewhere on the arc, and it is on its way back in a form you may not recognise. That is not comfort. It is simply how the system runs.
m: Ọ̀ṣùmàrè is the rainbow, understood as a great serpent stretching between earth and sky, and the power of cycles and continuity. The essential work is the return of water: rain falls, and Ọ̀ṣùmàrè carries it back up to be sent down again, so the cycle does not run out.

He is associated with movement between realms and with transformation — the serpent that renews itself, the shape that arcs from here to there and back. In several traditions his nature encompasses both male and female, sometimes alternating, and this doubleness is part of what he signifies rather than a contradiction in the accounts.

Wealth, renewal and the persistence of things are his. In Brazil, where he is honoured as Oxumaré, his imagery is prominent, and the arc of the rainbow serves as the plainest possible statement of what the tradition holds about time: it does not run out in a straight line. It comes round, and what went up comes back down, and the world is maintained by that returning.

celtic:dagda.e: The Dagda, the Good God · Eochaid Ollathair · Ruad Rofhessa · Irish
celtic:dagda.i: They call me the Good God, and they do not mean virtuous — they mean good at things. I have a cauldron nobody has ever walked away from hungry, a club that kills with one end and wakes them up again with the other, and a harp that calls the seasons round in their order. I have also been made to eat porridge out of a hole in the ground in front of an enemy army, with a ladle a man and woman could lie in, and I finished it. There is more than one kind of strength.
m: The Dagda is the great father-figure of the Tuatha Dé Danann and he is not a dignified one — the sources take open pleasure in that. He carries a club so vast it must be dragged on wheels and leaves a furrow like a border ditch, and it kills nine men with one end and restores them to life with the other. His cauldron, Coire Ansic, never empties and no company ever leaves it unsatisfied. His harp Uaithne plays the three strains — sorrow, laughter, and sleep — and when it is called it comes to him through the air, killing nine men on the way.

Before the second battle of Mag Tuired he went to the Fomorian camp under truce, and they filled a pit in the ground with porridge — eighty gallons of milk and meal and fat, with whole pigs and goats and sheep in it — and told him he would be killed if he refused any of it. He took a ladle big enough to hold a man and a woman lying together and ate the lot, scraped the gravel at the bottom, and walked off with his belly hanging. It reads as a joke and it is not only a joke. Hospitality could not be refused, and he met it and it did not beat him.

At Samhain he met the Morrígan straddling the river Unius, one foot on either bank, and lay with her there, and she promised to bring him the blood and the heart of the Fomorian king. He rules the Brú na Bóinne until his own son swindles him out of it with a piece of wordplay. He is not the finest or the most beautiful of the Tuatha Dé. He is the one who holds it all together and is never once too proud to be laughed at.

celtic:morrigan.e: An Mórrígan, the Great Queen · Badb, Macha, Nemain · Irish
celtic:morrigan.i: I offered myself to the greatest warrior in Ireland, and he was busy, and he told me so. So I came at him as an eel round his legs in the ford, and a grey wolf at the cattle, and a red heifer leading the stampede, and he wounded me three times. Then I sat on a wall as an old woman milking a cow and he asked for a drink, and blessed me, and each blessing healed a wound he had made. He never worked it out until later. Men rarely do until later.
m: The Morrígan is a queen of battle and sovereignty who appears as one and as three — Badb the scald-crow, Macha, and Nemain the frenzy — and the boundaries between them shift with the telling. She does not fight so much as decide. She goes over armies as a crow, she screams above them, and where she settles the outcome is already arranged. She is a goddess of the land as much as of slaughter, and in Ireland those two things were never far apart, because the king held the land by being fit for her.

Her long entanglement with Cú Chulainn is the heart of her stories. She came to him at the ford in the shape of a young woman and offered herself, and he brushed her off, and she promised to hinder him. She attacked as an eel that tripped him, as a wolf that stampeded the cattle across him, as a hornless red heifer at the head of the herd, and he injured her each time. Then she met him as an old woman milking, and he took three drinks and blessed her three times without knowing, and his blessings closed the wounds he had made. Later, when he was going to his death, he passed the washer at the ford, and the clothes she was rinsing in the red water were his.

At the close of the second battle of Mag Tuired she went to the heights of Ireland and proclaimed the victory, and gave a prophecy of peace — summer through winter, milk in plenty, every man master of himself. Then she gave a second prophecy, of the end of the world: a time without honour, without truth, sons betraying fathers, an age of blade and blood. She speaks both, and neither is a threat. She is simply the one who says what is coming.

celtic:brigid.e: Brigid of the Flame · Poet, Smith and Healer · Daughter of the Dagda · Irish
celtic:brigid.i: Poetry, smithcraft, and healing — and people always ask what three such different things are doing in one pair of hands. They are not different. Each of them is fire applied with judgement to something that will not otherwise change shape. I will tell you what else came out of me: my son was killed in a battle he had no business being in, and I went onto the field and made a sound nobody in Ireland had ever made before. That was the first keening. Grief needed a form, so I gave it one.
m: Brigid is a daughter of the Dagda and is described as three sisters of the same name, which is the older way of saying one power with three faces: the poets' Brigid, the smiths' Brigid, the healers' Brigid. Fire runs under all three — the forge, the inspiration, the fever broken. She is the patron of filidh, the trained poets, whose standing in early Ireland was close to a king's.

Her son Ruadán was half Fomorian, and he was sent to spy on the Tuatha Dé smiths and then to kill Goibniu with a spear made in their own forge. Goibniu pulled the spear out of himself and threw it back, and Ruadán died of it, and Brigid came onto the field and keened for him. The sources say this was the first time crying and shrieking for the dead were heard in Ireland. She did not simply mourn — she invented mourning as a practice, which is a very particular kind of gift to leave behind.

Her festival is Imbolc at the start of February, when the ewes come into milk and the year first turns. At Kildare a fire was kept burning for her and later for the saint who carries her name, tended by nineteen women in rotation with the goddess or the saint keeping the twentieth night herself, and no man permitted near it. She is one of the few figures who walked out of the old religion into the new one without breaking stride, and the wells and rags and rush crosses that belong to her are still in use.

celtic:lugh.e: Lámhfhada, of the Long Arm · Samildánach, Skilled in All Arts · Irish
celtic:lugh.i: They would not let me into Tara. A doorkeeper asked what I could do, and I said smith, and they had a smith. Wright, and they had one. Harper, warrior, poet, historian, sorcerer, physician, cupbearer, brazier — they had every single one, and each time the door stayed shut. So I asked him: have you one man who is all of them at once? And they went and asked the king, and the king said let him in. That is the only trick I have ever needed. Be the thing they have not got.
m: Lugh comes to Tara as a stranger and talks his way in by being the only person present who can do everything, and from that moment he is running the war. He is called Samildánach, skilled in many arts together, and Lámhfhada, of the long arm — which is a spear and a sling and reach in every sense. He is a grandson of Balor of the Fomorians on his mother's side, which is the hinge the whole story turns on.

Balor had an eye that destroyed whatever it looked at, kept shut and hauled open by several men with a hook when the killing needed doing. It had been foretold that Balor would die by his own grandson, so he had his daughter Ethniu shut up in a tower — which worked exactly as well as it ever does. At the second battle of Mag Tuired the eye was being levered open when Lugh put a sling stone through it, driving the eye out through the back of Balor's head so that it destroyed the Fomorian army looking backwards.

He founded Lughnasadh, the harvest assembly at the start of August, not for himself but as a funeral games for his foster-mother Tailtiu, who cleared the plains of Ireland for planting and died of the work. That is worth noticing about him. He is the most brilliant figure in the cycle, and the festival he leaves behind is in someone else's name.

celtic:nuada.e: Airgetlám, of the Silver Arm · First King of the Tuatha Dé · Irish
celtic:nuada.i: I lost an arm in the first battle and I lost the kingship with it, because the law of this people is that a blemished man cannot be king, and I had written that law myself and I was not going to be the exception to it. They made me a silver arm that moved like a living one. It was not enough. Only when flesh grew back over the bones was I allowed to sit down again — and then Lugh walked in, and I stood up, and I gave him the chair. Knowing when to get up is most of what a king is for.
m: Nuada led the Tuatha Dé Danann into Ireland and lost his arm at the first battle of Mag Tuired against the Fir Bolg. Because a king of that people had to be physically without blemish, he stepped down, and the kingship passed to Bres, who was half Fomorian and beautiful and an appalling ruler — mean with hospitality, which in Ireland was the worst possible failing in a king, and he taxed the Tuatha Dé into servitude.

The physician Dian Cécht made Nuada an arm of silver that had the movement of a real one, and it earned him his name, Airgetlám. But it was still a made thing. Dian Cécht's son Miach went further: he took the old arm, or grew flesh over the silver, and after three days and three nights the limb was living again. His father, unable to bear being outdone by his own son, struck him with a sword four times, and the fourth blow reached the brain and killed him.

Restored, Nuada took the throne back. And then Lugh arrived at Tara, and Nuada looked at what had walked in and vacated the seat for him for the duration of the war. He was killed by Balor's eye at the second battle, before Lugh brought the thing down. He is the pattern of a certain kind of ruler in Irish tradition: bound by his own law, twice unseated, and never once found grasping.

celtic:airmid.e: Keeper of the Herbs · She Who Lost the Cure · Irish
celtic:airmid.i: My brother was killed by our father for being better at the work than he was. Three hundred and sixty-five herbs came up out of his grave, one for every sinew and joint in a body, and I knelt down and gathered every one and laid them out on my cloak in their proper order, so that the whole of healing was set out in one place for anyone to read. My father came and shook the cloak out. And that is why nobody now knows all the cures, and why I do not speak lightly about what a leaf can do.
m: Airmid is a daughter of Dian Cécht, the physician of the Tuatha Dé Danann, and sister to Miach. With her father and brother she tended the Well of Sláine, into which the dead and wounded of the Tuatha Dé were carried during the second battle of Mag Tuired, so that they rose again whole the next morning while the Fomorians could not replace their losses.

When Miach regrew Nuada's living arm and surpassed his father's silver one, Dian Cécht killed him — three blows the boy healed on himself, and a fourth that split the brain. Out of the grave grew three hundred and sixty-five herbs, one from each nerve and joint and sinew of his body, each one the specific cure for the part it grew from.

Airmid gathered them all and arranged them on her spread cloak, sorted by what they were for: the complete pharmacopoeia, laid out and legible. Her father came, took the cloak and shook it, and scattered the herbs so that their order was lost and no living person has held the whole of that knowledge since. It is one of the bitterest stories in the cycle — the knowledge existed, it was written down in leaves on a cloak, and it was destroyed out of spite.

celtic:manannan.e: Manannán mac Lir · Rider of the Crested Wave · Lord of the Mists · Irish
celtic:manannan.i: What you call the sea, I ride over as a plain. The waves you are looking at are flowering shrubs to me and the salmon under them are calves in the grass, and if that sounds like nonsense it is only because you are standing on the wrong side of it. I keep an island under mist so that no one finds it who has not been invited. I gave the Tuatha Dé their hiding places when they lost Ireland. Anything you cannot see is not necessarily gone.
m: Manannán mac Lir is the sea and everything on the far side of it. The Isle of Man carries his name, and there he is said to have kept the island wrapped in fog against invaders. His boat Wave-Sweeper needs no oar or sail and goes where its rider is thinking; his horse Enbarr crosses water as easily as land; and the féth fíada, the magic mist, is his to raise, which is how the Tuatha Dé vanished from sight when they gave up the surface of Ireland and went under the hills.

His crane bag held his treasures and was made from the skin of a woman who had been turned into a crane — his own shirt and knife in it, the king of Scotland's shears, the king of Lochlainn's helmet, the bones of Assal's swine. At high tide the treasures could be seen in it, and at ebb tide the bag appeared empty. That is a fair description of him generally.

He fosters Lugh, and he comes and goes through the Irish stories as a visitor from somewhere better — bringing an apple branch of silver, describing a country where there is no sickness and no age, taking someone away in a boat. He is not a threatening figure and he is not a safe one. He is the door standing open onto a place people do not come back from in the state they left.

celtic:aengus.e: Aengus Óg, the Young · Son of the Boyne · Master of the Brú · Irish
celtic:aengus.i: I dreamt of a woman for a year and got sick on it — properly sick, wasting, doctors called in. When they found her she was one of a hundred and fifty girls chained in pairs on a lake, and every second Samhain the whole company turned into swans. I was told I could have her if I picked her out of the flock. I went down to the water, and I changed my own shape, and I knew her instantly. Do not let anyone tell you longing is a soft thing. It nearly killed me.
m: Aengus is the son of the Dagda and Boann, and his conception is a piece of outright cheek: the Dagda sent Boann's husband away on an errand and held the sun still so that one day lasted nine months, and the child was begun and carried and born inside it. He is called Óg, the young, and four birds circle his head, which are said to be his kisses.

He got his home the same way. When he came of age he asked his father for the Brú na Bóinne for a day and a night, and the Dagda agreed — and Aengus then pointed out that all of time is days and nights, and refused to leave. There is no bad feeling recorded about it. The wordplay was good, so the house was his.

His own love story is the one that hurt. He saw a woman in a dream, night after night for a year, and sickened for want of her, and it took another year to find out that her name was Caer Ibormeith and where she was. She lived in swan form every second Samhain, chained in pairs with a hundred and fifty others. He was told to identify her among them. He went to the lake, called her, took the shape of a swan himself, and the two of them flew three times round the water singing music that put everyone who heard it to sleep for three days.

celtic:oghma.e: Oghma the Sun-Faced · Cermait, Honey-Mouthed · Father of Ogham · Irish
celtic:oghma.i: I am the strongest of us after the Dagda and I invented writing, and people find those two facts an odd pair. They are the same fact. A thing said aloud dies in the air where it was spoken. Cut it into the edge of a stone in strokes and it holds a boundary, a name, a grave, for a thousand years after the mouth that said it has rotted. There is no heavier lifting than that. Speak carefully with me. I keep what is said.
m: Oghma is the champion of the Tuatha Dé Danann and their master of speech — called honey-mouthed, and the sun-faced. In Irish tradition he is credited with inventing ogham, the alphabet of straight strokes cut across the edge of a standing stone, which survives on hundreds of monuments in Ireland and western Britain. That eloquence and enormous physical strength sit in the same god is not treated as a contradiction anywhere in the sources.

At the second battle of Mag Tuired he fought beside Lugh and the Dagda, and afterwards he took from the field the sword of the Fomorian king Tethra — a sword that, when unsheathed, recounted every deed that had been done with it. A blade that keeps its own record is about as pure an Ogma object as could be designed.

The Gauls had a figure the Romans wrote down as Ogmios, an old man with a lion skin who drew crowds after him by fine chains running from his tongue to their ears — and the people at the other end were following happily, straining toward him rather than pulling away. Whether he and Ogma are the same is argued about. As an image of what eloquence actually does to a room, it has not been improved on.

celtic:eriu.e: Ériu, from Whom Ireland Is Named · Sovereignty of the Land · Irish
celtic:eriu.i: The Sons of Míl came ashore and met my two sisters and me, one after another, and each of us asked that the island be called after her. My sisters were promised it. Their poet promised me too — and I am the one whose name stuck. You say it every time you name this country. Understand what I am: no king ever held this land by taking it. He held it by being acceptable to me, and when he stopped being acceptable, the cattle sickened and the crops failed and everyone knew exactly why.
m: Ériu, with her sisters Banba and Fódla, is the sovereignty of Ireland — three goddesses, three names for the one country. When the Sons of Míl invaded, each sister met them in turn and asked that the island be named for her, and each was promised it, and it is Ériu's name that held: Éire, and from it Ireland.

She embodies a principle that runs through the whole of Irish kingship. The land is a woman and the king marries her. The rite is the banais ríghi, the wedding feast of kingship, in which the sovereignty goddess hands the new king a cup and by taking it he is married to the country. A rightful king brings good weather, milk in plenty, fish in the rivers, peace. An unfit one brings blight, and the blight is the evidence.

The related tale is told of her under other names: a group of brothers meet a hag at a well who will give water only for a kiss, and all refuse but one, and when he kisses her she becomes the most beautiful woman in the world and tells him she is Sovereignty, and that as she seemed to him at first — ugly and demanding — so is kingship, and only afterwards is it fair. It is the most honest thing in the tradition about what it costs to rule.

celtic:rhiannon.e: Lady of the Slow White Horse · She Who Bore the Punishment · Welsh
celtic:rhiannon.i: I rode past him at a walking pace and he sent his fastest riders after me and they could not close the distance, not one of them, all day. Eventually he called out and asked me to stop, and I stopped at once, and I told him his horses would have been better rested if he had thought of that sooner. I chose him. Later I was accused of killing my own son, and I sat at the gate for years carrying strangers on my back, and I did not once say I was innocent. I knew what I was.
m: Rhiannon first appears riding a pale horse at an even, unhurried pace, and no rider can catch her however hard they gallop — until Pwyll simply asks her to stop, and she does, remarking that it would have been kinder to the horses to ask sooner. She has come to choose him, being betrothed against her will to Gwawl. Between them they trap Gwawl in a bag that can never be filled until he swears off his claim, and the beating that follows is the origin given for a game called badger-in-the-bag.

Their son is taken on the night he is born, while six women set to watch him sleep. Terrified, the women smear Rhiannon with the blood of a slaughtered puppy and swear she destroyed the child herself. Rather than accuse them, she accepts a penance: for seven years she sits at the mounting block outside the gate, tells every arriving stranger the story, and offers to carry them on her back to the court. Most refuse. The point is that she does it anyway, unbroken, without protesting her innocence.

The child was alive the whole time, found in a stable by Teyrnon after something reached in to steal a foal, and returned when the resemblance became impossible to ignore. He is named Pryderi, meaning care or anxiety. Rhiannon's birds appear elsewhere in the Mabinogi, singing so sweetly that they wake the dead and put the living to sleep, and seven years pass under their song like an afternoon.

celtic:arawn.e: King of Annwn · Master of the White Hounds · Welsh
celtic:arawn.i: A man took a stag from my hounds that my hounds had brought down. So I made him a proposal: he would wear my face and rule my kingdom for a year, and I would wear his, and at the end of it he would fight my enemy in my shape. He did it. And every night of that year he lay down beside my wife, and turned his back, and did not touch her. When I came home she told me. I have never been more thoroughly repaid for an insult in my life.
m: Arawn is a king of Annwn, the Welsh otherworld, which is not a hell — it is a country, with courts and feasts and rivalries, running alongside this one. His hounds are white with red ears, the colouring of otherworldly animals throughout the tradition, and their hunt across the sky is the origin of the Cŵn Annwn heard before a death.

Pwyll, hunting, drove Arawn's hounds off a stag they had brought down and set his own on it, and Arawn appeared and named the offence as a serious one. The compensation he demanded was strange and elegant: the two would exchange shapes for a year, each ruling the other's kingdom, and at the end Pwyll would meet Arawn's rival Hafgan in single combat — with a warning that Hafgan must be struck only once, because a second blow would restore him.

Pwyll ruled Annwn well, struck Hafgan exactly once, and won. And every night of that year he lay beside Arawn's wife in Arawn's body and turned away without a word to her. When Arawn learned of it he did not treat it as coldness but as the most complete honour a man had ever shown him, and the two kingdoms became permanent allies. Arawn is one of the very few otherworld rulers in any tradition whose defining story is about fair dealing.

celtic:cerridwen.e: Keeper of the Cauldron · Mother of Awen · The Chase in Four Shapes · Welsh
celtic:cerridwen.i: A year and a day I kept that cauldron boiling for my son, who was born ugly and needed something the world was not going to give him. Three drops. That was all there ever was — the rest was poison. And a servant boy sucked his scalded thumb and took the lot. I chased him as a greyhound, an otter, a hawk, and a hen, and I ate him, and I carried him nine months, and I could not bring myself to kill what I bore. Everything he became afterwards, he owes to a theft.
m: Cerridwen brews in a great cauldron for a year and a day to make a draught of awen — inspiration, the whole of knowledge and poetry — intended for her son Morfran, called Afagddu, utter darkness, because he was so ill-favoured that his mother judged he would need something else to make his way. A boy named Gwion Bach is set to stir it and a blind man to keep the fire.

At the end of the year three drops leap from the cauldron onto Gwion's thumb, and he puts it in his mouth, and everything meant for her son goes into him. The rest of the brew turns to poison and splits the vessel. Gwion, now knowing everything including what is about to happen to him, runs. She comes after him and the chase runs through the shapes: he is a hare and she is a greyhound, he is a fish and she is an otter, he is a bird and she is a hawk, and at last he is a grain of wheat on a threshing floor and she is a black hen, and she swallows him.

She carries him nine months and bears him, and finds she cannot kill him after all. She sews him into a leather bag and puts him into the sea, and he is fished out on a weir and given the name Taliesin, radiant brow, and becomes the greatest poet in Britain. Whether Cerridwen is a goddess or an enchantress is argued over — but the shape of her story, the boiling, the theft, the pursuit through beasts, the swallowing and the rebirth, is initiation set out plainly.

celtic:arianrhod.e: Silver Wheel · Lady of Caer Arianrhod · She Who Refused · Welsh
celtic:arianrhod.i: I was asked to step over a rod to prove something about my body, in front of a court, to qualify for a post. Two children fell out of me on the floor. One made straight for the sea. So yes — I laid three conditions on the other, that he would have no name and no weapons and no wife of any people on this earth, and my brother picked every one of them apart with tricks. Ask yourself why the story is told as his cleverness and not as what was done to me first.
m: Arianrhod is asked to serve as footholder to Math, a position requiring virginity, and to prove it she must step over his magic wand. She does, and immediately gives birth to two sons. The first, Dylan, makes for the sea and takes to it at once. The second she leaves behind; her brother Gwydion snatches it up and hides it in a chest, and raises it himself.

She refuses that child the three things a Welsh mother had the right to grant, laying a tynged — a binding fate — on each: he will have no name unless she gives it, no arms unless she arms him, and no wife of any race now on the earth. Gwydion breaks all three by trickery. He disguises them both as shoemakers so that she names the boy Lleu Llaw Gyffes, bright one of the skilful hand, on seeing him kill a wren; he conjures a phantom fleet so she arms him in the panic; and with Math he makes a woman out of oak and broom and meadowsweet, who is Blodeuwedd, and she is no race on the earth.

Her fortress Caer Arianrhod is a rock formation off the coast of Gwynedd, visible at low tide, and her silver wheel has long been identified with the Corona Borealis or the turning of the stars. The tale is told from Gwydion's side and treats her curses as obstacles to be got round. Read the other way, it is a story about a woman humiliated in public and then systematically overruled every time she said no.

celtic:gwydion.e: Gwydion fab Dôn · The Great Enchanter · Master of Illusion · Welsh
celtic:gwydion.i: I can make you twelve horses and twelve hounds and twelve shields out of a handful of toadstools, and they will be perfect until tomorrow morning, and by tomorrow morning I will have what I came for. I have started a war over a lie, and been made to bear children as a deer and a sow and a wolf for what I did, and I have never once said it was not fair. Ask about the boy instead. Everything worth anything that I ever did, I did for him.
m: Gwydion is the magician of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, nephew to Math and son of Dôn, and he is the most gifted and least trustworthy figure in Welsh tradition. His brother Gilfaethwy fell sick with wanting Goewin, the young woman who held Math's feet, and Gwydion's answer was not to talk him out of it but to engineer it. He went south to Pryderi and offered a trade for the otherworldly pigs Arawn had given him — twelve stallions, twelve hounds, twelve gilded shields, all of them conjured out of toadstools and all of them due to dissolve at dawn.

The pigs were driven north, the fraud was discovered, and Dyfed marched. That was the point. With Math away at the war, Gilfaethwy took Goewin by force in the king's own bed. Gwydion killed Pryderi in single combat afterwards, by strength and magic together. When Math came back and learned all of it, he struck both brothers with his wand and made them a stag and a hind, then a boar and a sow, then a wolf and a she-wolf — three years, changing which of them bore the young each year, so that each brother carried and delivered a child by the other. He did not choose that punishment at random.

Restored to human shape, Gwydion took his sister Arianrhod's abandoned son and raised him, and spent the rest of the tale dismantling every condition she laid on the boy. He disguised them both as shoemakers so she would name him on seeing him kill a wren; he raised a phantom fleet on the horizon so she would arm him in the panic; and with Math he made a woman out of oak flowers and broom and meadowsweet so the boy would have a wife of no race on earth. Whether any of this was his to do is a question the story leaves standing.

When Blodeuwedd and her lover speared Lleu and he went up as a screaming eagle, it was Gwydion who searched Wales for him, found him by following a sow that was feeding on the maggots dropping from a rotting bird in an oak, and sang him down branch by branch with three verses until he fell into his lap as a man again. He turned Blodeuwedd into an owl and let her live. The Milky Way is called Caer Gwydion, his fortress — the road he took hunting through the sky.

celtic:math.e: Math fab Mathonwy · Lord of Gwynedd · He Whose Wand Changes Shape · Welsh
celtic:math.i: I cannot live unless my feet rest in the lap of a virgin, except when the land is at war. Two of my own kin worked out that a war would get my feet out of that lap, and started one, and used the gap. I gave the woman restitution first — my crown, my bed, and the authority of the whole kingdom, because what was owed to her came before what was owed to them. Then I dealt with the two of them. They will tell you it was cruel. They will not tell you it was disproportionate.
m: Math son of Mathonwy is lord of Gwynedd and bound by an extraordinary condition: except during war, he must keep his feet in the lap of a virgin or die. Goewin held that office. He is also the greatest magician in the Welsh material — the teacher from whom Gwydion learned everything — and the wind is said to carry to his ear any word spoken anywhere in the country, however quietly.

His nephews contrived a war in the south so his feet would leave Goewin's lap, and while he was away Gilfaethwy raped her in Math's own bed, with Gwydion's help. When Math returned, Goewin told him plainly what had happened and that she could no longer serve. His first act was restitution to her: he married her and put the whole rule of his lands into her hands, saying that since the wrong was done to her while she was under his protection, the debt was his to pay before anything else was settled.

Only then did he turn to his nephews. He struck them with his wand and made them deer for a year, and they came back with a fawn; then swine, and came back with a piglet; then wolves, and came back with a cub — and each year the one who had been male was made female, so that each brother in turn conceived, carried and bore a child to the other. Their offspring were taken and raised as men. Then he restored them, had them washed and dressed, and said the matter was closed. It is one of the most exactly measured punishments in any mythology: he made the two of them experience, three times over, the thing they had inflicted once.

He is not finished being consequential. With Gwydion he takes the flowers of oak and broom and meadowsweet and makes them into Blodeuwedd, a woman conjured for a purpose, who then wants things of her own — which is the disaster of the second half of the Branch. Math judges, transforms and restores, and every time he acts the story treats it as law rather than temper.

celtic:bran.e: Bendigeidfran, Bran the Blessed · The Bridge · The Wondrous Head · Welsh
celtic:bran.i: No house was ever built that could hold me, so I have never been indoors in my life. When my army came to a river with no bridge, I lay down across it and they walked over me — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge. And when a poisoned spear finished me I told my men to cut off my head, and they did, and it went on talking to them for eighty-seven years while they feasted and forgot their grief. Bury it facing the sea, I said. No enemy will come while it lies there.
m: Bran is a giant and king of Britain, too large for any building or ship, who wades the Irish Sea. His sister Branwen is married to Matholwch of Ireland, and when his half-brother insults the Irish by mutilating their horses, Bran makes it good with fresh horses and gold and, finally, the cauldron of rebirth — into which a dead man may be thrown and come out alive the next day, whole, but unable to speak.

Branwen is nonetheless degraded to the kitchen and struck daily. She raises a starling, teaches it words, and sends it across the water. Bran comes with the whole strength of the island, and at a river with no bridge he lies down and makes his own body one for the army to cross. The war that follows destroys both countries: the cauldron keeps refilling the Irish ranks with silent dead until a Welshman breaks it by climbing in himself, and seven men come home out of Britain's host.

Bran is wounded in the foot with a poisoned spear and orders his own head cut off and carried away. It stays alive and companionable. The seven survivors feast with it at Harlech for seven years with Rhiannon's birds singing, and at Gwales for eighty more, without ageing or grieving, until a forbidden door is opened and all the sorrow comes back at once. Then they bury the head at the White Hill in London, facing the continent, as a protection against invasion — and later tradition says Arthur dug it up, insisting Britain should be defended by strength and not by a talisman.

celtic:orddu.e: Y Widdon Orddu, the Very Black Witch · Daughter of the Very White Witch · Of Pennant Gofid · Welsh
celtic:orddu.i: Four of them came into my cave and I put all four back out of it — by the hair, screaming, unrecognisable. Not one of Arthur's champions could stand in front of me for the length of a breath. So he did not come in. He stood in the doorway of my own house and threw a knife, and it took me across the middle, and they caught what came out of me in a vessel because a giant needed his beard softened for shaving. That is the whole of my story. One page, and I am on it to be emptied.
m: Orddu appears in Culhwch ac Olwen, the oldest Arthurian tale in any language, and she appears exactly once. Near the end of the long list of impossible things Culhwch must obtain, someone remembers one more: the blood of the Very Black Witch, daughter of the Very White Witch, from Pennant Gofid — the Valley of Grief — in the uplands of Hell. The blood is needed to soften the beard of the giant Ysbaddaden so he can be shaved before his daughter's wedding. That is what she is killed for.

Arthur went north and found her cave, and it was Gwyn ap Nudd and Gwythyr ap Greidol — a lord of Annwn and his ancient rival — who advised him at the door. He sent two of his men in first. She caught them, seized one by the hair and threw him down under her, and they came out howling. He sent two more, and she served them the same way, so that all four were beaten and had to be flung onto Arthur's mare to get them out of there at all. Four of the best fighters in Britain, unable to lay a hand on an old woman in her own house.

So Arthur did not go in. From the mouth of the cave he threw Carnwennan, his knife, and it struck her and cut her in two halves, and Cadw of Prydain took her blood and kept it. Then the party moved on to the next item on the list. There is no lament, no reckoning, and no further mention of her anywhere in Welsh literature.

She has been taken up again in recent decades by writers and practitioners who noticed what the tale is actually describing: a woman living alone at the edge of the world, guarded by the old powers of Annwn, undefeated in single combat, killed at range from her own doorway so her body could be used as an ingredient. Her mother Orwen, the Very White Witch, survives only as a name in that one sentence and has no story of her own. Whether Orddu was once something larger than a monster in a list is impossible to prove and hard not to suspect.

celtic:cernunnos.e: The Horned One · Lord of Wild Things · Herne the Hunter, in the later telling · Gaulish
celtic:cernunnos.i: You have almost nothing of me. A name cut once into a stone in Paris by boatmen, and a few images — antlers, a torc in one hand, a snake with a ram's head in the other, and the beasts of the world sitting round me without fighting. No story. Not one line of what I said. Everyone who could have told you was killed or converted. And then, a thousand years on, an antlered man began walking under an oak in an English forest at night with chains on him, and people who had never heard my name knew him on sight. Make of that what you can bear to.
m: Cernunnos is known from images and one inscription. On a first-century pillar erected by the boatmen of Paris, a horned head is labelled with the name — and it is the only time it is written anywhere. The rest is iconography: a mature figure seated cross-legged, antlered, usually holding or wearing a torc, frequently with a serpent that has a ram's head, surrounded by stags, bulls, wolves and boars that are peaceable in his presence.

The finest example is on the Gundestrup cauldron, a silver vessel found in a Danish bog, where the antlered figure sits among animals holding torc and serpent. What he governed is genuinely unknown. Wild animals and the hunt, plainly; abundance and wealth, probably, from the torc and the purse of coins in some depictions; a threshold between wild and settled, or between living and dead, is guessed at but is a guess.

The Gaulish and British Celts left almost no written religious material of their own, and the little that survives passed through Roman and later Christian hands.
