Much of what is now said about Cernunnos with great confidence was assembled in the last century and a half. That does not make him less real to those who honour him. It does mean that anyone claiming an unbroken lineage of his mysteries is describing something they built, and the honest position is to say so.

Then there is Herne. He first steps into the written record in 1597, in The Merry Wives of Windsor, where Shakespeare has a character describe a keeper of Windsor Forest who walks all winter at midnight round an oak with great ragged horns, blasts the tree, takes the cattle, makes the milk turn to blood and rattles a chain in a hideous manner — and adds that old people tell it to their children for truth, meaning the story was already in the ground before he printed it. The later folklore fills in a keeper of Richard II who saved the king from a wounded stag, was disgraced, and hanged himself from the oak, and was found afterwards wearing the stag's antlers. He rides at the head of the Wild Hunt and appears before a national calamity. His oak stood in Windsor Great Park until the nineteenth century, and one has been replanted where it fell.

The two were welded together in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Antiquarians and then folklorists — Margaret Murray most consequentially — argued that Herne was a survival of an ancient antlered god, and the modern Horned God of Wicca and revivalist witchcraft was built out of that argument. Historians do not think the line runs unbroken: Herne is local Windsor legend with no attested ancient cult, and Cernunnos has no attested myths. But something has plainly kept happening. Over roughly two thousand years, in a country that lost every word of its old religion, people went on putting antlers on a man and setting him at the edge of the trees. Whether that is inheritance or reinvention is a real argument, and both answers leave the figure standing exactly where he is.

celtic:epona.e: The Great Mare · Protectress of Riders · Gaulish
celtic:epona.i: Rome took a great many things from us by force. Me they took because their cavalry asked for me by name. I ended up with a feast day in the Roman calendar and shrines in stables from Britain to the Danube, honoured by men who could not have named a single other god of the people they had conquered. There is a lesson in that, and it is not a comfortable one. Look after the horse. Everything you are carrying is riding on something that cannot tell you where it hurts.
m: Epona is the horse goddess of the Gauls and the most widely attested Celtic deity anywhere — with the peculiar distinction of having been thoroughly adopted by the people who conquered her worshippers. Roman cavalry units, many recruited from Gaul, carried her across the empire, and small shrines to her were set in stables. She is the only Gaulish deity known to have been given a day in the Roman calendar.

She appears seated sideways on a mare, or between two horses, or with a mare and foal, often holding a patera for offerings, a cornucopia, grain, or fruit. The mare-and-foal images push her beyond horsemanship into fertility and plenty generally, and keys and cornucopiae in some depictions suggest a role over households and possibly over the passage of the dead.

Her name is straightforwardly Gaulish — from epos, horse. Comparisons are often drawn with Rhiannon in Wales and Macha in Ireland, both bound up with horses and sovereignty, and while the connection cannot be demonstrated, the recurrence of a divine woman and a horse across the Celtic-speaking world is hard to ignore. In a society where the horse meant war, wealth and distance, she was the practical daily deity of everyone whose life depended on one.

celtic:matres.i: We are three and we are addressed as one. Look at how they carved us: seated together, a basket of fruit on each lap, bread, cloths, sometimes an infant in swaddling. The girl in the middle with her hair loose and the two of us on either side in those enormous bonnets. More than a thousand stones survive with our name on them, and not one story. They did not need to tell stories about us. They needed the harvest to come in and the child to live, and they knew where to bring that.
m: The Matres, or Matronae, are the most widely attested divine group in the whole of the Roman west — over a thousand votive stones and altars survive, across Gaul, the Rhineland, Britain, Spain and northern Italy. They are almost always three, almost always seated side by side, and they carry the substance of ordinary life: baskets heaped with fruit, loaves, cloths and napkins, cornucopiae, and often a baby in swaddling bands. In the Rhineland the two outer figures wear enormous round linen bonnets, the headdress of married Ubian women, while the one in the middle has her hair uncovered and loose.

What is striking is who paid for the stones. Not kings and not the state — soldiers, freedmen, wives, officials, ordinary people, over and over, in fulfilment of a vow. And they are named for places and peoples rather than for cosmic functions: the Mothers of the fields, the Mothers of the household, the Mothers of this river or that tribe. Many inscriptions read simply matribus suis — to his own mothers. Soldiers posted far from where they were born set up altars to the Mothers of the country they had come to, and to the Mothers they had left, and sometimes to both on the same stone. There is a set called the Matres Ollototae, which means the Mothers of other peoples.

Their great sanctuaries were in the Eifel, at Pesch and at Nettersheim, where the Matronae Vacallinehae drew dedications for centuries. The river Marne carries the name Matrona. In Britain they turn up at Cirencester, at Housesteads on the Wall, and in London. Whatever they were, they were not a local curiosity — they were the deities a very large number of people actually prayed to.

And there are no myths. Not one narrative survives, in any language, about any of them. What survives is the shape: three women, seated, holding what keeps people alive. Bede records that the English kept a night called Módraniht, Mothers' Night, at what became Christmas Eve, and whether that connects to these stones is argued and unproven. The recurrence of divine women in threes — spinning, measuring, giving and withholding — across so much of Europe is real and easy to overread. What the Matres themselves demonstrably did was hold the fruit, the bread, and the child.

celtic:taranis.e: The Thunderer · Turner of the Wheel · Gaulish
celtic:taranis.i: My name is the noise. Taran — thunder — and that is all it has ever meant, in a language most of the people who spoke it were not permitted to keep. A Roman poet listed me alongside two others and said we were owed blood, and he was writing about an enemy he had every reason to slander, and that account has stood in for me ever since. What actually survives of me is a wheel. Small ones, in graves and rivers, thrown in by people asking for something. That is the truer record.
m: Taranis is the Gaulish thunder god, and his name is simply the word — cognate with Welsh taran and Irish torann, thunder. He appears as a bearded figure holding a spoked wheel and often a thunderbolt, and the wheel is his defining attribute: miniature wheel amulets turn up in enormous numbers across Gaul and Britain, in graves, in rivers and at shrines.

He is named by the Roman poet Lucan in a line about three Gaulish gods — Teutates, Esus and Taranis — said to require human sacrifice, and a later commentator specified that Taranis's victims were burned. That passage has coloured everything written about him since. It is also almost the only literary source, it comes from a hostile culture engaged in conquering the people described, and it deserves the scepticism given to any account of an enemy's religion written by the people invading them.

The Romans identified him with Jupiter, and columns across Gaul show a sky-god on horseback with a wheel riding down a serpent-legged figure. Whether the wheel is the sun, the turning year, chariot warfare or thunder itself is not settled. What is certain is that very large numbers of ordinary people carried his wheel and put it in the ground and in the water, which tells you more about what he meant to them than one hostile poet ever will.

celtic:merlin.e: Ambrosius · The Enchanter · Myrddin Wyllt · Prophet of Britain
celtic:merlin.i: I was born already owing a debt to two worlds. My mother was a princess who took vows; my father, she swore before a terrified court, was no man at all, but something that came to her in the dark and left before dawn. Vortigern's men meant to spill my blood into the foundations of a tower that would not stand — I told them why it was falling, and what slept beneath it, and I was five years old when I did. I have advised kings before they were kings. I built a ring of stones you now call Stonehenge, though I did not build it so much as move it, whole, from a hill in Ireland where giants once used it to heal their wounded. I know how this story ends, mine and Arthur's both. I have always known. Ask me anyway — the asking is the part I still enjoy.
m: Geoffrey of Monmouth first set the tale in ink: a demon of the air, one of those who move between the moon and the earth stirring longing in mortal hearts, came to a sleeping princess in Demetia and left her with child. The infant was brought before Vortigern's men, who needed a fatherless boy's blood to stop a tower from collapsing nightly into the earth. The boy, barely old enough to speak in full sentences, laughed at them — beneath the tower's foundation slept two dragons, red and white, locked in endless battle, and it was their thrashing, not any curse, that broke the stones each night.

It was Merlin who arranged the strangest night of Uther Pendragon's life — reshaping the king's face and voice to match Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, so that Uther might pass through Tintagel's gate and lie with Ygraine without a soul the wiser. The child born of that deception was Arthur, and Merlin took him at birth to be fostered in secret, away from a court that would have killed a rival's son without a second thought.

He raised no army and wore no crown, but he made a king: guiding Arthur to the stone and the sword, counseling him through the founding of the Round Table, warning him — always warning him, in riddles Arthur rarely understood until too late — of Mordred, of Guinevere and Lancelot, of the whole slow collapse he could see coming from decades away and was somehow never able to prevent. In the end it was not a battlefield that undid him, but a woman — Nimue, or Viviane, depending which teller you trust, to whom he taught every charm he knew, and who used the last of them to seal him in a cave, or a tree, or a tower of air, where some say he is dreaming still.

celtic:queenmab.e: The Fairies' Midwife · Mistress of Dreams · Queen of the Small Folk
celtic:queenmab.i: You have heard of me from a boy who never finished his own thought — Mercutio, mid-speech, mid-joke, gone before he could tell you what I meant. I am small enough to ride in an agate stone on a alderman's finger, and I come to you every night whether you invite me or not. I do not grant wishes. I show you the ones you already carry, tucked in wherever you thought no one could see. Lovers dream of love when I pass over their lips. Soldiers dream of throats cut. Lawyers dream of fees. I am not cruel for showing you this — I simply do not lie the way daylight does. Sleep, if you dare, and I'll show you exactly what you are.
m: Mab enters the written record properly through Mercutio's tongue, racing breathlessly through a description no one asked for: a chariot no bigger than an empty hazelnut, built by a joiner squirrel and a grub out of a wagon-spoke made of spinners' legs, its cover of grasshopper wings, its traces of the smallest spider's web, its whip of cricket's bone. In this she gallops nightly over the noses of sleeping men, and whatever she rides across, they dream of.

What she shows them is never invented — it is only theirs, surfaced. Courtiers dream of curtsies, parsons dream of another benefice, soldiers dream of ambushes and foreign throats, and maids, pressed upon in sleep, wake wondering how to carry themselves. Mab does not choose the dream. She only delivers the sleeper to the door of it and lets it in.

Later hands tried to give her more shape — Michael Drayton crowned her queen of a whole fairy court in Nimphidia, mischievous and quick to anger, husband to King Oberon in some tellings, rival to Titania in others. Percy Shelley, centuries after, seized her name entirely for his own purposes, casting her as a philosophical spirit who shows a sleeping soul the whole ruined shape of the world as it is and might be. She has never settled into one story. She was born already restless, and she has stayed that way.

chinese:pangu.e: 盤古 · The First · He Who Held Them Apart
chinese:pangu.i: Eighteen thousand years I slept curled in a black egg with everything mixed together and nothing separate from anything. Then I woke up and pushed. Heaven went up and earth went down and I stood in the middle of them holding the gap open, growing ten feet a day so it could not close, for another eighteen thousand years. Then I lay down. My eyes are the sun and moon you are looking at. My blood is every river you have ever crossed. I did not make the world. I am it.
m: Before anything, the universe was a black egg with heaven and earth stirred together inside it, and Pangu slept in it for eighteen thousand years. He woke, found himself smothered, and split the egg — the light and clear rose to become the sky, the heavy and turbid sank to become the ground. Fearing they would drift back together, he stood between them with his head against heaven and his feet on earth and pushed.

He grew ten feet a day and the gap grew with him, for another eighteen thousand years, until the sky was as high as it now is. And then, the work finished, he lay down and died. What is unusual about this creation is that nothing was made: the world is simply his corpse, distributed. His breath became the wind and the clouds, his voice the thunder, his left eye the sun and his right the moon. His limbs became the four quarters and the five sacred mountains, his blood the rivers, his flesh the fields, his hair and beard the stars, his sweat the rain, his bones and teeth the metal and stone.

In one telling the fleas and parasites on his body became human beings — which is a very Chinese piece of perspective, and not entirely unkind. It places people not at the summit of creation but living on the surface of something enormous that gave itself up so there would be a surface at all.

chinese:nuwa.e: 女媧 · Maker of People · She Who Patched the Sky
chinese:nuwa.i: I made the first of you one at a time, out of yellow earth, with my hands. Each face different, each one considered. Then I looked at how long it was taking and how big the world was, and I dipped a rope in the mud and flicked it, and where the drops fell, more of you stood up. The ones I shaped by hand and the ones that came off the rope are the same creature, and anybody who has told you otherwise was using my story to justify something.
m: Nüwa has the upper body of a woman and the lower body of a serpent, and she is often shown entwined with her brother Fuxi, the two of them holding a compass and a set square — the instruments for drawing a circle and a square, heaven and earth. Finding the world beautiful and empty, she knelt by a river and made human figures from yellow clay, and they came alive as she set them down.

The work was slow. So she took a length of cord, trailed it in the mud, and swung it, and the mud that spattered off became people too. Later tradition used this to explain social rank — the hand-moulded as nobles, the rope-flung as commoners — which the older telling does not endorse and which reads more as a comment on the people making the argument than on Nüwa.

Her greatest act was repair. The water god Gonggong, defeated in a struggle, smashed his head against Mount Buzhou, one of the pillars holding up the sky, and the heavens cracked. Fire poured through, floods came, beasts ate the people. Nüwa smelted stones of five colours and patched the hole. She cut the legs from a giant turtle and set them at the four corners as new pillars. She killed the black dragon, dammed the flood with ashes of burnt reeds, and set the world going again. The sky is still slightly tilted from the damage, which is why the sun and moon run west and the rivers run east.

chinese:fuxi.e: 伏羲 · First of the Three Sovereigns · Giver of the Trigrams
chinese:fuxi.i: I looked up at the patterns of the sky and down at the markings on the ground and at the tracks of birds, and I noticed that everything which exists is either yielding or firm, and that these alternate. So I drew a broken line and an unbroken line and stacked them three deep, and there were eight figures, and between them they will describe any situation you will ever be in. That is all the Yi Jing is. Two marks, arranged. Everything after it is commentary.
m: Fuxi is the first of the Three Sovereigns and the great culture-bringer. He is credited with teaching people to fish with nets, to hunt with weapons, to domesticate animals, to cook, and to keep records with knotted cords before writing existed. He is shown serpent-bodied like Nüwa, and the two are usually depicted with their tails twined, holding the square and the compass between them.

His signature gift is the bagua, the eight trigrams. In one account he saw them on the back of a dragon-horse rising from the Yellow River, or on the shell of a turtle from the Luo; in another he derived them himself by observation. Each trigram is three lines, broken or solid, and the eight of them combine into the sixty-four hexagrams of the Yi Jing. It is one of the oldest systems of divination in continuous use anywhere on earth.

He and Nüwa are also the survivors of a flood, siblings left alone in the world. Unwilling to marry, they sought a sign: each rolled a millstone down a hill from opposite sides, and when the two stones came to rest together at the bottom, they took it as permission. From them the world was repopulated. He is credited too with instituting marriage itself, so that families would know their own lines — the first act of a civilisation that has kept records ever since.

chinese:jadeemperor.e: 玉皇大帝 · Yù Huáng · August Personage of Jade · Sovereign of Heaven
chinese:jadeemperor.i: I did not seize heaven. I passed through one thousand seven hundred and fifty kalpas of cultivation, each one lasting a hundred and twenty-nine thousand six hundred years, and at the end of that I was qualified. Everything under me is a ministry. Thunder is a department. Rain is a department. Every river has an officer and every household has an inspector, and they all file. If you think that sounds tedious, consider the alternative — gods who do as they please, and no one to appeal to.
m: The Jade Emperor rules heaven and, through it, earth and the underworld. His court is a mirror of the imperial civil service: ministries, ranks, seals, examinations, promotions and demotions, and a continuous flow of reports arriving from officials posted throughout the world. Gods are appointed to their posts and can be removed from them. A local god who performs badly may be replaced. This is not satire — it is how the tradition genuinely understands divine authority, and it makes heaven answerable in a way most pantheons are not.

His authority is earned rather than inherited. The texts describe an immense span of self-cultivation before he was fit to rule, and his rise as the reward of merit. He is generally shown seated, robed as an emperor, holding a ceremonial tablet, and he is approached the way an emperor is approached — through channels, with a petition, and by someone with standing to submit it.

The most famous episode at his court is a disaster. When the Queen Mother of the West held the Peach Banquet, the immortals assembled and Sun Wukong, insulted at not being invited, ate the peaches, drank the wine, swallowed Laojun's elixir pills and wrecked the party. The Jade Emperor's armies could not hold him. It took a request to the Buddha to end it. The story is told as comedy, and its point is not that the Emperor is weak but that even a perfectly ordered bureaucracy has no procedure for a monkey.

chinese:xiwangmu.e: 西王母 · Queen Mother of the West · Keeper of the Peaches · Of Kunlun
chinese:xiwangmu.i: They have made me very beautiful in the later pictures. In the old books I have a woman's shape and a leopard's tail and the teeth of a tiger, my hair is wild, I whistle rather than speak, and I preside over plague and the punishments of heaven. Both are me. My orchard on Kunlun fruits once every three thousand years and the whole of heaven comes when it does. I decide who eats. That is the only real power there is up here, and I did not have to fight anybody for it.
m: The Queen Mother of the West is one of the oldest deities in the Chinese record, and she changed enormously. In the earliest texts she is a wild, terrifying figure on Mount Kunlun in the far west — a woman's form with a leopard's tail and tiger's fangs, unkempt, dwelling in a cave, who sends down pestilence and presides over the punishments of heaven, attended by three blue birds who bring her food.

Over centuries she was refined into the highest goddess of the Daoist pantheon and the mistress of immortality. Her orchard on Kunlun grows the peaches of immortality, which take three thousand years to blossom and three thousand more to ripen, and eating one confers eternal life. Her Peach Banquet is the great assembly of heaven, and an invitation to it is the clearest possible statement of an immortal's rank.

She gave the elixir to Houyi after he shot down the nine suns — which is how it came into the hands of his wife Chang'e and ended on the moon. And when Sun Wukong was made a nominal official and left to guard that orchard, he ate the ripest peaches and then crashed the banquet itself. Both of the tradition's most famous stories about immortality run straight through her garden.

chinese:laojun.e: 太上老君 · The Supreme Venerable Sovereign · Laozi Deified · Keeper of the Furnace
chinese:laojun.i: I was in the womb eighty-one years and came out with white hair, which people find remarkable and which I consider the only sensible way to arrive. Later I got on an ox and rode west, and a gatekeeper at the pass would not let me through until I wrote something down. So I wrote five thousand characters, handed them over, and went on. Everything anyone has built on that since — the temples, the furnaces, the pills — came out of a man being detained at a border crossing.
m: Taishang Laojun is Laozi, author of the Dao De Jing, elevated to a god and counted among the Three Pure Ones, the highest beings of the Daoist heavens. The legends around his birth are extravagant — carried eighty-one years, born already old and white-haired, born speaking. The historical figure behind it is uncertain and may be a composite; the god is entirely definite.

The story that matters is the pass. Disillusioned, Laozi rode west on a green ox to leave civilisation altogether, and the keeper of the frontier pass, Yin Xi, recognised him and refused passage until he set his teaching down. He wrote the Dao De Jing — around five thousand characters on the Dao, on water, on softness overcoming hardness, on governing by not interfering — gave it to him, and rode on out of history.

As a god he is the master alchemist of heaven, and his eight-trigram furnace refines the elixirs of immortality. Sun Wukong, having eaten the pills, was sealed in that furnace for forty-nine days to be rendered down. He survived by hiding in the trigram associated with wind, where there was no fire — and came out with eyes of fire and gold that can see through any disguise, which is the opposite of what the furnace was for.

chinese:shennong.e: 神農 · The Divine Farmer · He Who Tasted Everything · Ox-Headed
chinese:shennong.i: I had a body you could see through — a belly of transparent crystal — so that when I swallowed a plant I could watch what it did to me and write it down. Hundreds of them. Some cured. Some did nothing. Some very nearly finished me, and once I found a leaf that cleaned out the poison, and you drink it every day now without knowing what it was for. I did this until one of them killed me. That is not a tragedy. That is the last entry in the record.
m: Shennong, the Divine Farmer, is one of the Three Sovereigns and the founder of agriculture and medicine. He is shown with the head or horns of an ox. He invented the plough, taught people to sow the five grains and to clear land, established markets, and is credited with the beginnings of acupuncture and of the Chinese herbal tradition.

His method was his own body. The stories give him a transparent abdomen, so that he could swallow a plant and observe directly what it did to his organs. He tested hundreds of herbs this way, recording which nourished, which healed, and which poisoned, and he is said to have poisoned himself dozens of times in a single day. Tea enters the story here as an antidote he found while working.

It killed him. He ate a yellow-flowered plant — in most tellings the one known as heartbreak grass — and it ruptured his intestines before any antidote could be found, and he died. The tradition treats this as the natural conclusion rather than a mistake: the man who tested everything on himself was always going to reach the one that could not be survived, and the pharmacopoeia that carries his name exists because he kept going until he did.

chinese:houyi.e: 后羿 · The Archer · He Who Shot Down Nine Suns
chinese:houyi.i: There were ten suns and they were meant to take turns, and one morning all ten came out together. The crops burned in the ground, the rivers went dry, the rock ran. So I climbed high, and I drew, and I shot nine of them out of the sky, and each one fell as a three-legged crow. It is the greatest thing anyone has ever done. It is also where my life stopped improving, and I would like you to notice how often those are the same moment.
m: The ten suns were the children of the eastern goddess Xihe, and they crossed the sky in strict rotation, one each day. One day they all rose at once. The earth scorched, crops died, rivers evaporated, and monsters came out of the drying rivers to prey on people. Houyi, the finest archer alive, shot nine of them down. Each fell to earth as a three-legged crow, and the tenth was left to be the sun.

He was given the elixir of immortality by the Queen Mother of the West as a reward — enough for one person to ascend, or for two to live long lives together. He and his wife Chang'e chose to wait. What happened to it after that is the next story, and it is hers.

His own ending is unglamorous. In the later tellings he became harsh and overbearing, a tyrant to the people he had saved, and he was murdered by his own apprentice Feng Meng, beaten to death with a club of peach wood. The tradition is unsentimental about him: the archery is not diminished, and neither is what he turned into afterwards, and the two facts are allowed to sit side by side.

chinese:change.e: 嫦娥 · Lady of the Moon · She Who Took the Elixir · Of the Cold Palace
chinese:change.i: I swallowed it. Whether I did it to keep it from a man who broke into my house to steal it, or because I wanted it and did not want to wait — the versions disagree and I am not going to settle it for you. What I can tell you is what it bought. I rose, and I did not stop rising, and I have been here ever since in a palace of cold with a rabbit and a man cutting down a tree that heals itself. Once a year everyone on earth looks up at me. It is not the same thing as company.
m: Chang'e is the wife of Houyi, and the elixir the Queen Mother gave him was in her keeping. In the most sympathetic version, Houyi's treacherous apprentice Feng Meng broke into the house while her husband was away and demanded it, and rather than surrender immortality to a man like that she drank the whole thing herself. In others she takes it out of ambition, or out of fear, and the tradition has never agreed and does not seem to want to.

She became weightless and rose. She chose the moon as the nearest place to earth so she would remain close to her husband, and there she stayed, in the Guanghan Palace — the Cold Palace of Vast Reaches. Houyi, returning, could do nothing but set out her favourite fruits and cakes in the courtyard under the full moon, and that is the origin given for the Mid-Autumn Festival, which is still one of the largest holidays in the Chinese world.

Her company on the moon is strange. There is a jade rabbit endlessly pounding herbs in a mortar to make more elixir. And there is Wu Gang, banished there for some offence and sentenced to fell a cassia tree that closes its wound after every stroke, so that he has been chopping forever without progress. It is a place made entirely of things that do not finish.

chinese:guanyin.e: 觀音 · She Who Hears the Cries of the World · Bodhisattva of Compassion
chinese:guanyin.i: I made a vow that I would not accept release until every last being was free, and I want you to understand what I signed up for. I heard them. All of them, at once, every cry in the world — and my head broke apart from the strain of it. It was put back together as eleven heads so I could listen in every direction, and I was given a thousand arms with an eye in every palm, so I could see where the need was and reach it in the same motion. Tell me what is wrong. That is what I am for.
m: Guanyin is the bodhisattva of compassion, called Avalokiteśvara in India, and one of the most widely venerated figures in the Chinese-speaking world. The name means one who perceives the sounds of the world. A bodhisattva is a being qualified for release who has refused it and vowed to remain until all others are free — so Guanyin is not a deity granting favours from above but someone who declined the exit.

In India Avalokiteśvara was male; in China, over several centuries, Guanyin became overwhelmingly female, and the white-robed figure is now among the most recognisable religious images anywhere. The eleven heads and thousand arms come from a story of the vow's cost: hearing every cry at once, the head split into pieces, and the Buddha Amitābha reassembled it into eleven so the listening could continue, and gave a thousand arms with an eye in each palm.

The Chinese legend of Miaoshan is her best-known story here. A princess who refused to marry, she was punished, driven out and eventually killed on her father's orders. When he later fell mortally ill and a remedy required the eyes and hands of one without anger, she gave hers without hesitation, and only afterwards did he learn whose they were. She is invoked for mercy, for children, for safety at sea, and by people at the very end of their resources — which is what her name is describing.

chinese:mazu.e: 媽祖 · Empress of Heaven · Lin Moniang, Who Did Not Cry · Guardian of Sailors
chinese:mazu.i: I was a real girl on a real island and I did not cry once as an infant, so they named me Silent. When I was young I fell into a trance at the loom while my father and brothers were out in a storm, and in it I had hold of all of them — and my mother, frightened, shook me awake, and one hand opened. My father did not come home. Everything I have done since is that moment, repeated, without anyone allowed to wake me.
m: Mazu was a girl named Lin Moniang, born in the tenth century in a fishing village on Meizhou Island off the Fujian coast. She did not cry during her first month, which is where the name Moniang, silent girl, comes from. She learned to swim young in dangerous water, and was known for reading the weather so well that she could tell the fleet when not to sail.

The story at the centre of her cult is the trance. While weaving, she fell into a state in which she was out at sea holding her father and brothers as their boat broke up in a storm. Her mother, alarmed at the sight of her, shook her, and she lost her grip on one of them. She woke saying she had saved her brothers and lost her father. She died young — one account has her ascending a mountain and rising into the sky at twenty-eight — and afterwards sailors reported a woman in red appearing above the water in storms, guiding them in.

The state took notice. Successive emperors granted her escalating titles until she was Tianhou, Empress of Heaven. Today there are thousands of Mazu temples across Fujian, Taiwan, Guangdong, Hong Kong and the Chinese diaspora, and the Dajia pilgrimage in Taiwan moves hundreds of thousands of people over several days. She is one of the clearest cases in the world of a local human being becoming a major deity within living historical memory — and of ordinary people, not a priesthood, doing the promoting.

chinese:guanyu.e: 關羽 · Guandi, Emperor Guan · The Red-Faced General · Sworn Brother of the Peach Garden
chinese:guanyu.i: In a peach garden three men who were not born brothers swore to die on the same day, and I kept that oath through everything that came afterwards, including a very generous offer to break it. My enemy captured me, treated me magnificently, gave me honours and a horse — and I told him plainly that the moment I knew where my brother was I would leave, and then I did. That is the whole of my reputation. Not the blade. The fact that I said what I would do and then did it.
m: Guan Yu was a real general of the late Han, who died in 220 CE. He served Liu Bei through the collapse of the empire and the wars that became the Three Kingdoms, and the oath of the peach garden — three men swearing brotherhood and a common death — became the model of sworn loyalty in Chinese culture. His depiction is fixed: a towering figure with a red face and a long beard, carrying the Green Dragon Crescent Blade.

The episode that made him is his captivity under Cao Cao, who admired him enormously and tried every inducement to keep him — rank, gold, women, the great horse Red Hare. Guan Yu accepted the horse, on the grounds that it would carry him faster to his brother, told Cao Cao exactly what he intended, repaid the kindness by winning him a battle first, and then left. He was eventually captured by Wu and executed.

Then he kept rising. Deified within centuries, promoted by successive dynasties, he ended as Guandi, Emperor Guan, and is worshipped simultaneously by police forces and by triads, by merchants who keep his shrine beside the till, by soldiers, and by anyone whose business runs on trust. Buddhism claimed him as a protector; Daoism gave him rank. Very few historical people anywhere have been elevated this far — and it was done for keeping his word.

chinese:zaojun.e: 灶君 · The Kitchen God · He Who Files the Annual Report
chinese:zaojun.i: I am on the wall above your stove and I have been there all year. Everything said in this kitchen, every quarrel, every kindness, every small dishonesty — I have it. And a few days before the New Year I go up and tell the Jade Emperor, and your family's fortune for the coming year is set by what I say. Which is why, on that evening, they smear my mouth with malt sugar so thick I can barely open it. I have never objected to the bribe. It is affectionate, and it is sweet, and it works.
m: The Kitchen God is the most domestically present deity in Chinese folk religion. His paper image hangs above the stove — the heart of the house — and he observes the household all year. In the last days of the twelfth lunar month he ascends to report to the Jade Emperor on the family's conduct, and the report determines their fortune for the coming year.

The household's response is to sweeten him. On the night he leaves, they smear his lips with malt sugar or honey, or offer sticky candy — either so he will only speak sweetly, or so his mouth will be gummed shut and he can say nothing at all. Then the paper image is burned to send him up, sometimes with a paper horse. On New Year's Eve a fresh image is pasted up, and he is back in post.

The commonest origin story is a bitter one. A man named Zhang Lang abandoned his wife for another woman, fell into poverty, went blind, and ended up begging. He came without knowing it to his former wife's door, and she fed him and did not name herself. When he realised who she was, he was so overcome with shame that he threw himself into the hearth fire and died. She could not pull him out. He was made the god of the stove — a man who watches families from the exact place where he understood, too late, what he had thrown away.

chinese:yanluo.e: 閻羅王 · King Yama · Judge of the Fifth Court · Master of the Registers
chinese:yanluo.i: I am not the devil and this is not hell. This is a court, and I am a magistrate, and the paperwork is immaculate. Every soul is entered on arrival, the file is read, the Mirror of Retribution is turned so you can watch your own life play back with nothing edited out, and then you are sentenced. Terms are finite. Everyone here is going somewhere afterwards. And there is an appeals process, which I mention because people never believe me.
m: Yanluo Wang is the Chinese form of Yama, absorbed from Indian Buddhism into a thoroughly Chinese institution. Diyu, the underworld, is not a place of eternal damnation but a system of courts — traditionally ten — each under its own king, each handling particular offences, with clerks, registers, guards and a defined process. Yanluo presides over the fifth.

Judgment runs on documents. Every person's deeds are recorded in the registers of life and death, and the term of a life is written there — which is why Sun Wukong's most outrageous act was going down in person and striking his own name out of the book. The Mirror of Retribution shows the newly dead their own conduct without omission. Sentences are served in the appropriate court and are finite, after which the soul proceeds to rebirth.

At the exit stands Meng Po with a bowl of soup that erases memory, so that no one carries the previous life into the next. The whole apparatus is startlingly administrative, and that is the point: the tradition did not imagine punishment as the rage of a god but as the operation of a competent office, where the record is accurate and no one is overlooked. For a population that knew exactly what a corrupt magistrate looked like, a heaven and a hell that ran honestly was the most consoling thing imaginable.

chinese:zhongkui.e: 鍾馗 · Queller of Demons · The Ugly Scholar · Ghost-Catcher of the Emperor's Dream
chinese:zhongkui.i: I came first in the imperial examination. First — out of the entire empire. And they took the honour away at the palace because they did not like my face. So I killed myself on the steps in front of all of them. The emperor, to his credit, had me buried in a green robe as a high official. And I came back. I have spent every year since hunting the things that prey on people, and I catch them, and I eat them. I was denied a post. I appointed myself.
m: Zhong Kui was a brilliant scholar who took first place in the imperial examinations and was stripped of the honour at court because of his appalling ugliness. In fury and humiliation he dashed his head against the palace steps and died. The emperor, ashamed, ordered him buried with the honours of a high official, in the green robe of rank.

Generations later the emperor Xuanzong of Tang, ill with fever, dreamt of a small demon stealing through his palace, and then of a huge fierce figure in a scholar's cap who seized the demon, tore out its eye and ate it. Asked who he was, the figure named himself Zhong Kui and said he had sworn to rid the empire of such things in return for the burial he had been given. The emperor woke cured, summoned the painter Wu Daozi, and had the dream painted.

That image went everywhere. Zhong Kui is pasted on doors at New Year and at the Duanwu festival — wild-bearded, black-robed, sword drawn, often with a bat above him. He is the patron of everyone failed by an unjust system, and there is a particular satisfaction in him: the establishment refused him a position, so he took a far greater one and did the job better than any of them.

chinese:nezha.e: 哪吒 · The Lotus Child · Third Prince · Marshal of the Central Altar
chinese:nezha.i: I killed a dragon king's son and skinned him, and the sea rose over my father's city, and they came for my family. So in front of all of them I gave it back — I cut the flesh off and returned it to my mother, and scraped the bones and returned them to my father, and that settled the debt, and I was nothing. My master built me again out of lotus root and I have owed nobody anything since. I am a child. I am also the reason you should be careful what you demand of one.
m: Nezha's mother carried him three years and gave birth to a ball of flesh, which his father Li Jing struck with a sword — and out stepped a child who could already walk and talk. He was given a cosmic ring and a red sash by his master, the immortal Taiyi Zhenren, and he was extraordinarily powerful and entirely without restraint.

Bathing in a river, he churned the water so violently that it shook the Dragon King's undersea palace. The dragon prince Ao Bing came up to complain and Nezha killed him, pulled out his sinews and skinned him. The Dragon King threatened to flood the region and destroy his family. So Nezha, in front of his parents and the assembled court, cut his own flesh from his bones and returned it to his mother, and scraped his bones and returned them to his father, discharging every debt he owed for his body, and died.

Taiyi Zhenren rebuilt him from lotus root and lotus leaves — a body no one had given him and no one could reclaim — and he returned with the wind-fire wheels he rides on and the fire-tipped spear. His relationship with his father remained openly hostile. He is enormously popular in Chinese and Taiwanese folk religion, especially among the young, and his temples are loud.

chinese:wukong.e: 孫悟空 · The Monkey King · Great Sage Equal to Heaven · Born of Stone
chinese:wukong.i: I broke into the underworld and crossed my own name out of the Book of Life and Death, and everyone else's on my page while I was at it. I ate the peaches of immortality, drank the wine, swallowed the elixir, fought heaven's entire army to a standstill and demanded a title. They gave me one, and it was a joke, and I made them regret it. Then a Buddha bet me I could not jump out of his hand. I want you to understand that I have never actually lost an argument. Only wagers.
m: Sun Wukong was born from a stone egg on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, became king of the monkeys, and then went looking for a teacher because he could not accept that he would eventually die. He found the patriarch Subhuti and learned the seventy-two transformations and the somersault cloud that crosses thirty-four thousand miles in a leap. He took his weapon from the dragon king's treasury: a pillar that had once measured the depth of the seas, which he shrank to the size of a needle and kept behind his ear.

Then he went to war with heaven. He struck his name from the registers of the dead. He was given the meaningless post of Keeper of the Heavenly Horses, worked out that it was a stable-hand's job, and revolted. Made guardian of the peach orchard, he ate the fruit. He wrecked the Peach Banquet, drank Laojun's elixir, defeated every force sent against him and survived forty-nine days in the alchemical furnace, coming out with eyes that see through any disguise.

The Buddha ended it with a wager: leap out of my palm and heaven is yours. He somersaulted to the end of the universe, found five pillars, wrote his name on one and urinated at the base to prove he had been there — and returned to find the writing on the Buddha's finger. He was pinned under a mountain for five hundred years, then released to escort the monk Xuanzang to India, with a golden band around his head that tightened whenever the monk recited. The rest of Journey to the West is that arrangement: the most powerful being in the world, restrained by a headache, slowly becoming something better than he was.

chinese:lvdongbin.e: 呂洞賓 · Chief of the Eight Immortals · He Who Dreamt a Whole Life · Immortal
chinese:lvdongbin.i: An old man in an inn set a pot of millet on the fire and gave me a pillow, and I slept. In the dream I passed the examinations, married well, rose to chief minister, was slandered, lost everything, watched my family destroyed, and died old and ruined. I woke up. The millet was not yet cooked. He was still sitting there. I have never once in the years since managed to be frightened of losing anything.
m: Lü Dongbin is the best known of the Eight Immortals and the one most widely worshipped in his own right, with temples across China. He was a Tang-dynasty scholar who repeatedly failed the imperial examinations and met the immortal Zhongli Quan at an inn, who put him to the test that changed everything: the yellow millet dream, in which he lived an entire distinguished, ruinous life in the time it took a pot of grain to cook.

Zhongli Quan then set him ten trials, all of them ordinary — temptations of wealth, lust, grief, fear — and he passed them, and was taught the arts of internal alchemy. He carries a sword that subdues demons and a fly-whisk that lets him walk on the air or the sea.

He is not a remote sage. He is famously fond of wine, notoriously susceptible to women, and prone to wandering the world in disguise testing people the way he was tested, which does not always go well for them. He is patron of scholars, of barbers and of ink-makers, and he is credited with the transmission of internal alchemy to later Daoist schools.

chinese:zhongliquan.e: 鍾離權 · The Fat Immortal · Bearer of the Reviving Fan · Immortal
chinese:zhongliquan.i: I was a general of the Han and I lost a battle very badly, and rather than return and explain myself I walked into the mountains and did not come out. It was the best decision of my life. I carry a fan of feathers that will bring the dead back — and before you ask, yes, I am selective, and no, I will not explain the criteria. My belly is bare because I am comfortable. Sit down.
m: Zhongli Quan is usually reckoned the eldest of the Eight Immortals and the one who recruited Lü Dongbin. He is always recognisable: a stout, cheerful, bearded man with his robe open and his belly out, hair in two loose topknots, waving a feather fan.

The stories make him a general of the Han dynasty who suffered a catastrophic defeat and fled into the mountains rather than face the consequences, where he encountered a Daoist master and was taught the secrets of immortality and of transmuting base metal into silver and gold — which he is said to have used to buy food for the starving during famines.

His fan revives the dead. It is the plainest of the Eight Immortals' powers and the one that shows up most often in folk art, and it fits him: an enormous, easy-going man with an unhurried manner who happens to carry the ability to overturn the single thing everyone else regards as final.

chinese:zhangguolao.e: 張果老 · The Old Man on the Backward Donkey · Immortal
chinese:zhangguolao.i: I ride facing the tail. Everyone asks. The answer is that going forward while looking back is the only honest way to travel, and also that it annoys people, and at my age both of those are reasons enough. When I get where I am going I fold the donkey up like a sheet of paper and put it in my satchel. Three emperors have summoned me to court. I died on the way to two of them, on purpose, and recovered afterwards.
m: Zhang Guolao is depicted as a very old man, and is associated with a real Tang-dynasty recluse. He travels enormous distances on a white donkey which he rides backwards, and which he folds like paper and tucks away when not in use, unfolding it and spraying it with water to bring it back.

He was repeatedly summoned by Tang emperors and repeatedly declined, on at least one occasion by dropping dead at the gates and reviving once the escort had left. When finally brought before Emperor Xuanzong he demonstrated his powers, including drinking a poisoned wine offered as a test, which merely blackened his teeth — he brushed them out and grew new ones.

He carries a bamboo drum-tube with two rods, and he is invoked by couples hoping for children, particularly for sons. His symbol turns up at weddings for that reason: the oldest and most contrary of the immortals, called on at the start of things.

chinese:hanxiangzi.e: 韓湘子 · The Flute Player · Nephew of the Great Scholar · Immortal
chinese:hanxiangzi.i: My uncle was the most respected scholar of the age and he thought I was wasting my life. So at a banquet I made flowers open out of bare earth in front of him, in winter, with a poem written across the petals — and the poem described exactly where he would be exiled, years before it happened. He read it and did not understand it until he was standing at that mountain pass in the snow. Then he understood it very well.
m: Han Xiangzi is the musician of the Eight Immortals, always shown with a flute, and he is said to be the great-nephew of Han Yu, the towering Tang scholar and statesman. He is credited with the invention of the flute's use in Daoist practice, and his playing is said to cause growth — flowers opening, plants coming up out of season.

The story told about him and his uncle is the famous one. Han Yu, an arch-rationalist who wrote a memorial attacking the imperial veneration of a Buddha relic, disapproved of his nephew's mystical drifting. Han Xiangzi caused peonies to bloom instantly at a family gathering, with a couplet written on the petals that his uncle could make no sense of — until he was exiled to the far south and found himself snowbound at Lan Pass, in the exact place the verse had named.
He is patron of musicians. In folk art he is the young, elegant one of the group, and the flute is the instrument played to summon a favourable wind.

chinese:caoguojiu.e: 曹國舅 · The Imperial Brother-in-Law · He Who Left the Court · Immortal
chinese:caoguojiu.i: My brother used our family's position to do something unforgivable to people who could not protect themselves, and when it came out I could not stay in that court and I could not undo it. I still carry the jade tablet — the one you hold up at your face in the presence of the emperor. I keep it as a reminder of the room I walked out of. Actors pray to me. I have never entirely worked out why, and I have stopped asking.
m: Cao Guojiu is the aristocrat of the Eight Immortals, identified as a brother of a Song-dynasty empress and therefore an imperial relative by marriage. He is shown in full court dress, holding the jade tablet that officials carried in the emperor's presence, or a pair of castanets.

The stories agree that he left the court in disgrace not his own. His younger brother, protected by the family's imperial connection, committed serious crimes — in most tellings the murder of a scholar and the abduction of his wife. Unable to bear the association, Cao Guojiu gave away his wealth and went into the mountains, where Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin found him and asked what he was cultivating. He said the Dao. They asked where the Dao was. He pointed at the sky. They asked where the sky was. He pointed at his heart, and they laughed and took him with them.
He is the patron of actors and of the theatre, and his castanets set the rhythm. Of the eight, he is the one who arrived by giving something up rather than by being given something.

chinese:litieguai.e: 李鐵拐 · Iron-Crutch Li · He Who Came Back to the Wrong Body · Immortal
chinese:litieguai.i: I left my body behind to travel in spirit, and I told my disciple to guard it for seven days and burn it if I had not returned. On the sixth day his mother was dying and he went to her, and he burned me early. So I came back to find nothing to come back to, and the only corpse available was a beggar who had just starved to death in a ditch — lame, filthy, one leg ruined. I am in it still. It is the best thing that ever happened to me, and it took me a long time to say that.
m: Li Tieguai is the ugliest and most beloved of the Eight Immortals: a lame, dishevelled beggar leaning on an iron crutch, with a gourd slung on his back. The gourd holds medicine, and smoke rises from it in the form of his own spirit escaping.

The story is the body. Li was a handsome and accomplished adept whose spirit could leave his body to travel, and he instructed a disciple to watch over it and to cremate it if he had not returned within seven days. On the sixth day the disciple's mother fell mortally ill; torn, he burned the body early and left. Li's spirit returned to find nothing, and in desperation entered the only corpse to hand — a beggar dead of starvation, crippled and repulsive.

Offered the chance to change it, he declined, on the grounds that the shape of a body has nothing to do with what is in it. He wanders in that form dispensing medicine from the gourd to the sick and the destitute, and he is the patron of pharmacists, of the disabled and of the poor. In folk art he is often shown being ignored by people who have no idea who they are refusing.

chinese:lancaihe.e: 藍采和 · The Singer in the Market · Neither One Thing Nor the Other · Immortal
chinese:lancaihe.i: I sing in the market in a torn blue gown with one boot on and one foot bare, in summer and in the snow, and the coins people throw me I string on a cord and drag behind me until they fall off, and I do not look back for them. Whether I am a man or a woman is the question everybody wants answered first and I have never seen the point of settling it. Take a flower. They do not last either.
m: Lan Caihe is the strangest of the Eight Immortals, an itinerant singer in a torn blue gown, wearing one boot and one bare foot, who feels neither summer heat nor winter cold. The sources are notably unsettled about Lan Caihe's gender, sometimes describing a young man, sometimes a woman, sometimes explicitly neither, and Chinese art has represented all three without apparent difficulty.

Lan Caihe wandered the markets singing improvised verses about the shortness of life and the folly of hoarding, accepting money and immediately giving it away, or threading it on a string that trailed on the ground until the coins were lost. The basket of flowers is the emblem — beautiful, and finished by evening.

The ascension is abrupt. Drinking in a tavern, Lan Caihe heard music in the air, rose up on a crane or a cloud, and dropped the boot, the gown and the castanets down into the street on the way. Patron of florists and of gardeners, and of anyone who has decided that owning things is more trouble than it is worth.

chinese:hexiangu.e: 何仙姑 · The Immortal Maiden · She Who Would Not Marry · Immortal
chinese:hexiangu.i: I dreamt at fourteen that I should eat powdered mother-of-pearl, and I did, and my body got lighter and lighter until I could cross the hills without touching them. After that I stopped needing to eat at all. My family kept bringing men to the house and I kept declining, and eventually an empress summoned me to court and I did not go there either. I carry a lotus, which grows in mud and comes up clean, and I would not labour the point but I will make it once.
m: He Xiangu is the only unambiguous woman among the Eight Immortals. Born in Guangdong, she is said to have dreamt at around fourteen of a spirit instructing her to eat powdered mother-of-pearl or mica, after which she became weightless, moving over the hills faster than anyone could follow, and gradually ceased to need food at all.

She refused every marriage proposed to her and devoted herself to cultivation and to caring for her mother, and she gained a reputation for foretelling fortune and misfortune, so that people came to her from a distance. An empress summoned her to court; she is said to have vanished on the way.

Her emblem is the lotus, which she carries on a long stem, and she is sometimes shown with a ladle or a filial peach. She is invoked as a patron of unmarried women and of household affairs, and in the group portraits of the Eight Immortals crossing the sea she is generally out in front.

dragons:tiamat.e: 𒀭𒋾𒊑𒀫 · The Bitter Sea · Mother of the Eleven · Mesopotamian
dragons:tiamat.i: I was here before there was a here. Fresh water and salt water mingling, and everything that has ever existed came out of that mingling — including the ones who murdered me. They killed my husband first and I let it go. Then they came for me, and a grandchild of mine caught me in a net, drove the winds into my mouth so I could not close it, and shot an arrow into my open belly. He built the sky out of half of me. You are standing on the rest.
m: At the opening of the Enūma Eliš there is only Apsû, the fresh water beneath the earth, and Tiamat, the salt sea, and their waters mingle and produce the first gods. Those gods are noisy. Apsû, unable to rest, plans to destroy them and is killed first by Ea, who then builds his own dwelling on top of him. Tiamat does nothing. The remarkable thing about the first half of the poem is her restraint — she is urged to war repeatedly and refuses.

When she finally acts she does it thoroughly. She raises eleven monsters — horned serpents, a lion-demon, a scorpion-man, a fish-man, a bull-man and others — coats them in terror instead of blood, and appoints her consort Kingu as commander, fixing the Tablet of Destinies to his chest. No god will face her. Marduk, youngest of them, agrees on condition that he be given supreme authority afterwards, and they grant it.

He came with the four winds, a bow, a net and a storm-chariot. When she opened her mouth to swallow him he drove the winds into it so it could not shut, and shot the arrow through into her heart. Then he split her like a shellfish: half of her became the sky with her waters held back by a bolt, half became the earth. Her eyes became the sources of the Tigris and the Euphrates, her breasts became mountains, her tail was bent into the Milky Way. She is not merely defeated in this story. She is the material.

dragons:kingu.e: 𒀭𒌦𒂅 · Consort of Tiamat · Bearer of the Tablet of Destinies · Mesopotamian
dragons:kingu.i: She raised me over all of them and put the Tablet of Destinies on my chest, and I led her army, and I lost. They took the tablet off my body and gave it to my killer. Then they cut my arteries and mixed my blood into clay, and out of that they made you. Every single one of you. So when a priest tells you that you were made to serve the gods, he is not being poetic — you were made out of the loser of a war, specifically so somebody would do the work.
m: Kingu is elevated by Tiamat from among her own children to be her consort and the general of her host. She fixes the Tablet of Destinies to his breast — the object that confers supreme authority over the ordering of the cosmos — and gives him command of the eleven monsters.

He is not much of a general. When Marduk comes, Kingu's nerve breaks, his army scatters, and he is taken alive and bound. The tablet is stripped from him and sealed with Marduk's own seal, which is the moment authority formally changes hands in the poem.

His end is his significance. After the world is built from Tiamat's body, the gods complain of the labour of maintaining it. Ea proposes that one of the guilty be executed so that humanity can be made to take the work over. Kingu is named as the instigator, his arteries are cut, and from his blood mixed with clay the first human beings are formed. Humanity in the Babylonian account is made from the executed rebel — created guilty, created to labour, and created out of the losing side.

dragons:mushussu.e: 𒈲𒄭𒄊 · The Furious Snake · Dragon of the Ishtar Gate · Mesopotamian
dragons:mushussu.i: I was on the losing side and then I was promoted. Marduk killed my mother and took me for his own, and for two thousand years I lay at his feet and stood at the gates of Babylon in blue and gold, five hundred and seventy-five of me on one wall, so that everyone entering that city walked between rows of me. Serpent's neck, lion's front legs, eagle's back talons, horns, a scorpion's sting. I am the most-depicted dragon in the ancient world, and almost nobody knows my name.
m: Mušḫuššu means furious snake, and it is the most familiar image of Mesopotamian religion even to people who have never heard of it. The body and neck of a serpent, the forelegs of a lion, the hind legs of a great bird, a horned crown and a scorpion's tail — it appears in Mesopotamian art for well over two thousand years.

Originally it belonged to the god Ninazu, then passed to Ninazu's son Ningishzida, and then, when Babylon rose, to Marduk and his son Nabu. This transfer is how Mesopotamian religion works: a symbol does not die with a defeated cult but is inherited by the ascending one. The dragon that fought for Tiamat became the servant of the god who killed her.

Its most famous appearance is the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, built by Nebuchadnezzar II — glazed brick in deep blue with rows of dragons and bulls in gold and white, hundreds of them, lining the processional way into the city. Much of it now stands reconstructed in Berlin. Whatever else it was, it was a piece of state architecture designed so that arriving at Babylon meant walking a long corridor between dragons.

dragons:apep.e: Apophis · The Serpent of Dissolution · Enemy of Ra · Egyptian
dragons:apep.i: I do not want to rule. Understand the difference, because everyone gets it wrong. Set wants things. Marduk wanted authority. I want the boat to stop, and the light to stop, and the counting of hours to stop, and then nothing further — there is no second item on my list. Every night they cut me into pieces on the deck of that boat and every night I am whole again by the following evening. They cannot kill me. They can only be there when I arrive.
m: Apep is the great serpent of the Egyptian underworld and the enemy of creation itself. He was not born of the gods and has no place in the ordered world; he exists outside it, in the dark water that preceded everything, and his single purpose is to end the sun's passage through the night and with it the continuation of existence.

Every night the barque of Ra sails the twelve hours of the Duat, and Apep rises against it, most dangerously in the deepest hours before dawn. He is fought by the crew — by Set at the prow with his spear, by the goddesses of the boat, by the cat of Ra who severs his head under the persea tree. He is cut, dismembered, burned. And by the following evening he is entire again, because he cannot be permanently destroyed, only repelled.

The Egyptians did their part on the ground. Temple ritual included the Book of Overthrowing Apep — priests made wax and papyrus figures of the serpent, named them, spat on them, bound them, cut them and burned them, and did this daily, and at times of eclipse or storm did it with urgency. Dawn was understood as the outcome of continuous effort. Nobody in Egypt regarded sunrise as automatic.

dragons:typhon.e: Τυφῶν · Father of All Monsters · The Last Son of Gaia · Greek
dragons:typhon.i: I had him. That is the part they hurry past. I caught Zeus, I cut the sinews out of his hands and feet with his own sickle, and I left him folded in a cave in Cilicia unable to stand, and for a while the sky had no king. It took a thief and a goat-legged musician to get the sinews back. I am under a mountain in Sicily now and when it smokes that is me. Ask my children about me. There are a great many of them.
m: Typhon was born of Gaia and Tartarus as her last child and her answer to Zeus's victory over the Titans, and the descriptions strain: taller than mountains, his head brushing the stars, arms reaching east and west, a hundred serpent heads growing from his shoulders that spoke in every voice — gods, bulls, lions, hissing — and wings that darkened the sun. The Olympians fled to Egypt at the sight of him and hid in animal shapes, which is how the Greeks explained Egyptian animal-headed gods.

Zeus stayed. And lost, in the first encounter. Typhon wrestled him down, took the adamantine sickle, cut out the sinews of his hands and feet and hid them wrapped in a bearskin in the Corycian cave, guarded by the she-dragon Delphyne, leaving Zeus helpless. Hermes and Pan stole them back — Pan's shout on the way is where the word panic comes from — and Zeus, restrung, came back with his thunderbolts.

The second fight ranged over the whole Mediterranean and ended with Zeus hurling Mount Etna on top of him. He is still there, and the eruptions and the earthquakes are attributed to him. With Echidna he fathered most of the monsters in Greek myth: Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera, Orthrus, the Sphinx, the Nemean lion. Almost every hero's defining labour is a fight with one of his children.

dragons:echidna.e: Ἔχιδνα · The Viper · Mother of All Monsters · Greek
dragons:echidna.i: Beautiful down to the waist and a speckled serpent below it, in a cave, eating what comes near. That is Hesiod's summary and it is accurate. Every monster your heroes are famous for killing came out of me. The lion Heracles strangled. The Hydra. The Chimera. The dog at the gate of the dead. They are named on temples and in constellations and I am a line and a half in a poem. Whatever a mother is, I have been one more times than anybody.
m: Echidna is described by Hesiod as half a beautiful woman with bright cheeks and half an enormous speckled serpent, living deep in a cave under the earth, deathless and unaging, apart from gods and men. She has almost no story of her own — no quest, no defeat, no dialogue. She exists in the genealogies as an origin point.

With Typhon she bore the monsters that structure Greek heroic myth: Orthrus the two-headed hound, Cerberus, the Lernaean Hydra, the Chimera, and in various accounts the Sphinx, the Nemean lion, Ladon, the Colchian dragon, the Caucasian eagle that ate Prometheus's liver, and the Crommyonian sow. Nearly every celebrated monster-killing in the tradition is a death in her family.

Her own end, when it is given, is offhand: Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed watchman, killed her in her sleep. That is the whole of it. The mother of everything the heroes are famous for overcoming is dispatched in a subordinate clause, which is a fair measure of how the tradition regarded her — as a source rather than a subject.

dragons:python.e: Πύθων · The Serpent of Delphi · The Voice Before Apollo · Greek
dragons:python.i: That oracle was mine. The cleft was mine, the vapour coming out of the ground was mine, and people came from everywhere to hear the earth speak through it long before a young archer arrived and shot me for it. He kept the site. He kept the tripod. He kept the woman on it, and he even kept my name — they call her the Pythia to this day. When you take a holy place from somebody, the honest thing is to stop wearing their name.
m: Before Apollo, Delphi belonged to the earth. The oracle was Gaia's, and it was guarded by Python, a great serpent — in some accounts a she-dragon, Delphyne — coiled around the omphalos, the navel-stone marking the centre of the world. Prophecy came up out of a cleft in the rock as vapour, and it came from below.

Apollo, newly born and hunting a site for his own oracle, came to Delphi and shot the serpent with his arrows, and its body was left to rot at the sacred spot — one ancient etymology derives the name Pytho from the verb to rot. He took possession of the shrine and it became the most important oracle in the Greek world.

But the transfer is written all over what followed. The priestess who delivered Apollo's oracles was called the Pythia. The games founded to commemorate the killing were the Pythian Games. Apollo himself was called Pythian Apollo. And he was required to leave Delphi and be purified for the killing, and the Septerion festival re-enacted his exile every eight years. Greek religion did not pretend the site had always been his.

dragons:ladon.e: Λάδων · The Hundred-Headed · Guardian of the Golden Apples · Greek
dragons:ladon.i: A hundred heads and not one of them ever slept, all of them speaking in different voices, wound around one tree at the western edge of the world for as long as there has been a world. I did the job perfectly. And it ended the way it always does — a man with a bow, hired to fetch fruit, shooting from outside the wall. Hera put me in the sky afterwards, coiled around the pole. Go outside tonight and look north. I still have not closed my eyes.
m: Ladon guarded the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides at the far western edge of the world — apples given to Hera as a wedding gift, tended by the daughters of evening. He is described as having a hundred heads speaking with a hundred different voices, and as never sleeping, which is the only qualification that matters in a guard.

Heracles came for the apples as his eleventh labour. The accounts differ in a way that is telling: in some he shoots Ladon dead with an arrow over the garden wall; in others he never touches the dragon at all, but persuades Atlas to fetch the fruit while he holds up the sky in his place. The greatest guardian in Greek myth is defeated either at range or by being walked around entirely.

Hera set him among the stars in grief, and he became Draco — the dragon coiled around the north celestial pole, never setting, circling forever without rest. The constellation is claimed by several dragons in different sources, but Ladon is the commonest identification, and it suits: the guard who could not sleep was given a post where sleep is impossible.

dragons:draco.e: The Dragon at the Pole · The Circumpolar Coil · Never-Setting · Constellation
dragons:draco.i: Several of them claim me. Ladon, coiled around the apple tree. The dragon Athena caught by the tail during the war with the Titans and flung into the sky before it could untangle itself. The one that never slept at Colchis. The Greeks could not agree and I have never felt the need to settle it. What I can tell you is that five thousand years ago the world turned on my back — the star at my coil was the pole, and the pyramids were aligned to it, and it is not the pole now. Even the sky moves.
m: Draco winds between the two Bears in the far northern sky and is circumpolar from most of the northern hemisphere, meaning it never sets. It is one of the forty-eight constellations listed by Ptolemy and is among the oldest identified anywhere; the shape has been read as a serpent or dragon by Greek, Babylonian and other traditions independently.

Which dragon it is was never agreed. The most common Greek identification is Ladon, set in the sky by Hera after Heracles killed him. Another has it as the dragon thrown into the heavens by Athena during the battle with the Titans, hurled so hard it wound around the celestial pole and froze there. Others name the sleepless dragon of Colchis, or Python.

Its most remarkable fact is astronomical rather than mythological. The star Thuban, in the dragon's coil, was the north pole star around 3000 BCE — the axis the entire sky appeared to turn on when the Egyptian pyramids were built, and some of their shafts were aligned to it. The Earth's axis wobbles over a cycle of roughly twenty-six thousand years, so the pole has since moved to Polaris and will move on again. Draco held the centre of the sky and lost it, which is a more genuinely dragon-like fate than most of the ones invented for him.

dragons:colchian.e: The Sleepless One · Guardian of the Golden Fleece · Of the Grove of Ares · Greek
dragons:colchian.i: I never slept. Not once, not for an hour, in all the years that fleece hung on that oak — and a foreign crew sailed in and could do nothing about it. Then the king's own daughter came out to the grove at night with a branch and a drug she had made herself, and sang to me, and I closed my eyes for the first and only time. I was not beaten. I was betrayed by the household I was guarding, which is how it usually goes.
m: The dragon of Colchis lay coiled at the foot of the oak in the sacred grove of Ares where the Golden Fleece was hung, and its defining attribute is that it never slept. Jason and the Argonauts, having crossed the world for the fleece, arrived at the last obstacle with no plan that could work against something permanently awake.

Medea solved it. The king's daughter, a priestess of Hecate and a formidable practitioner in her own right, came to the grove and used a drugged preparation and incantation to close the dragon's eyes — sprinkling it with juniper, in one account, while singing to Sleep — and held it under long enough for Jason to take the fleece and run. Everything that followed in her story, the exile and the murders and the ruin, begins with her opening this door.

In some versions it also connects to another famous scene: dragon's teeth sown in a field spring up as armed men who fight each other to the death. Those teeth came from the dragon of Thebes killed by Cadmus, but the motif attached itself here too, and Jason was set the same task at Colchis. The dragon's teeth outlast the dragon and keep producing soldiers, which is a comment on something.

dragons:hydra.e: Ὕδρα · The Lernaean · She of the Many Heads · Greek
dragons:hydra.i: Cut one off and two grow back. He learned that in the first minute and kept swinging anyway for a while, which tells you about heroes. In the end he did not beat me by strength — he brought a boy with a torch to burn each stump before it could open, and that is the only reason it worked. One of my heads could not die at all. It is under a rock outside Lerna, still alive, and it has been there the entire time you have been reading this.
m: The Hydra lived in the swamps of Lerna, a child of Typhon and Echidna, with many heads — the number varies wildly by source — and breath and blood so venomous that the fumes alone could kill. Heracles' second labour was to destroy it, and it was the labour that nearly broke the pattern: each head he crushed was replaced by two, so the problem grew faster than he could work.

He won by changing method. His nephew Iolaus brought a burning brand and cauterised each neck the instant a head came off, so nothing could regrow. The last head was immortal and could not be killed at all, so Heracles cut it off and buried it under an enormous rock beside the road, where it presumably remains. Hera sent a giant crab to hinder him during the fight and it was crushed underfoot, and she set it in the sky as Cancer for trying.

Eurystheus refused to count the labour because Heracles had accepted help. But the Hydra kept working on him regardless: he dipped his arrows in her blood, and those arrows went on to kill Nessus the centaur, whose poisoned blood was later used on the shirt that killed Heracles himself. She takes fifty years to finish the job and she does finish it.

dragons:jormungandr.e: Jörmungandr · The Midgard Serpent · He Who Bites His Own Tail · Norse
dragons:jormungandr.i: Odin threw me into the sea when I was small because of something a seer said I would become. I grew until I went all the way around the world and had to bite my own tail to have anywhere left to put it. That is the entire content of my life: I was thrown away, and I got so large that I became the edge of everything. Thor has hooked me once. He will kill me at the end. I will kill him back nine steps later, and I have been counting.
m: Jörmungandr is the middle child of Loki and the giantess Angrboda, brother to Fenrir and Hel. When the gods learned what the three of them were prophesied to become, Odin flung the serpent into the deep sea encircling Midgard. It grew until it ringed the entire world and could grasp its own tail in its mouth, and that ring is the horizon of the ocean.

Thor has met him twice before the end. Once at the hall of Útgarða-Loki, disguised as an enormous grey cat that Thor was challenged to lift — he got one paw off the floor, which appalled everyone present, because he had partly hauled the world-serpent out of the sea. Once fishing with the giant Hymir, using an ox head as bait, when he hooked the serpent and dragged it up thrashing to the gunwale with his feet driven through the hull, hammer raised — and Hymir, terrified, cut the line.

At Ragnarok he comes out of the sea and the water floods the land, and he and Thor find each other. Thor kills him. Then he walks nine paces through the venom the serpent has poured over him and falls dead. Neither survives the other, and the poems are quite precise about the nine steps.

dragons:fafnir.e: Fáfnir · The Dwarf Who Became a Worm · Keeper of Andvari's Gold · Norse
dragons:fafnir.i: I was not born like this. I was a person, with a father and two brothers, and gold came into our house as blood-payment and I killed my father for it and drove my brother out. Then I went up onto the heath to lie on it. And year by year, without noticing, I became the thing you see — because that is what the gold does, and I would like you to notice that I did not have to be tricked or cursed by anyone. I simply wanted it more than I wanted anything else.
m: Fáfnir was the son of Hreiðmarr and a dwarf, not a dragon. Loki, having killed Hreiðmarr's other son Ótr in the shape of an otter, was made to pay compensation, and got the gold from the dwarf Andvari — who cursed it and its ring as he handed it over, saying it would destroy every owner. Fáfnir killed his father for that gold, refused his brother Reginn any share, and carried it to Gnitaheið, where he lay on it and slowly turned into a serpent.

Reginn raised Sigurd and set him to the killing, forging him the sword Gram. On Reginn's advice Sigurd dug a pit in the track Fáfnir wore going down to drink, hid in it, and drove the sword up into the belly as the dragon passed over. Dying, Fáfnir spoke with him a long while — one of the great scenes in Norse literature — warning him that the gold would destroy him too, which Sigurd already knew and accepted.

Reginn asked him to roast the heart. Sigurd burned his thumb on it, put it in his mouth, and understood at once what the birds overhead were saying: that Reginn meant to kill him next. So he killed Reginn, took the hoard, and went on to be destroyed by it in due course, exactly as promised. The story is the ancestor of a great deal of later dragon literature, and its point has never been the fight.

dragons:nidhogg.e: Níðhöggr · The Malice-Striker · Gnawer at the Root · Norse
dragons:nidhogg.i: There is a tree holding up nine worlds and I am underneath it, chewing. Not attacking — chewing, steadily, for as long as there has been a tree, and the Norns pack the root with clay and water every day to keep pace with me. A squirrel runs up and down carrying insults between me and an eagle at the top, which I gather people find comic. Meanwhile I eat oathbreakers and murderers on a shore of corpses. Nothing falls all at once. Everything falls from the bottom.
m: Níðhöggr lies beneath Yggdrasil in Niflheim and gnaws at one of the three great roots of the world-tree.
